CP-005:
The four Appellate Division departments had divided between treating the films as the plaintiff's own statements and treating them as litigation-preparation materials. The railroads stressed impeachment: advance viewing might let a plaintiff tailor testimony. The plaintiffs stressed authenticity: editing, camera angle, speed, lighting and selective chronology can distort an apparently objective record.

The court found substantial need in authenticating potent visual evidence before it influenced the jury. Cross-examination at trial might not expose distortion, careful examination could require an expert and a substantial continuance, and later disproof might not undo the film's initial impact. The plaintiff's knowledge of his own condition was not a substantial equivalent, because the film memorialized conditions and a moment that could not likely be replicated; that satisfied undue hardship. The court recognized a genuine risk of tailored testimony but rejected the premise that films are necessarily accurate and plaintiffs necessarily dishonest, and balanced the concern by requiring disclosure only after the plaintiff's deposition.

In Poole, disclosure designed to prevent ambush did not permit the plaintiff to turn the defendant's choice not to use the films into prejudicial jury argument. That summation, the handling of the foreman's absence and the restrictions on the vocational evidence cumulatively denied a fair trial. A footnote disavows Reehil to the extent it said exceptions to improper summation comments present no reviewable legal question.

The casebook's editorial note explains that within a year the Legislature enacted CPLR 3101(i), requiring disclosure of all covered material including outtakes, that Tai Tran held this also displaced the deposition-first requirement, and that Zegarelli confirmed both changes. The brief concludes that the qualified protection and deposition-first sequencing are therefore historical rules, not the operative New York standard.

CP-007:
Klaxon required the federal diversity court to use New York's conflict rules. Those rules selected Pennsylvania law for substantive tort issues but New York law for procedural issues, and New York required plaintiffs in a nonfatal-injury action to prove freedom from contributory negligence. The instruction was therefore wrong.

The then-existing Rule 51 required a distinct objection to an instruction before the jury retired, stating the matter and the grounds, so that the trial judge has a meaningful chance to reconsider and correct the charge. An exception taken when no instruction ruling was before the court did not serve that purpose. The panel distinguished cases about the specificity of an objection actually made at the charge, cases involving preserved evidentiary rulings, and Keen, where additional preserved error justified reversal. This was not an exceptional case warranting correction of an unpreserved error.

On the speed instructions, the judge read the Pennsylvania statute and had explained that contributory negligence would bar recovery; the requested language was not wholly accurate and was too dogmatic, and a judge need not adopt counsel's formulation where the jury receives sufficient law. On rehabilitation, the proposed rule allowed consistent statements made before a motive to fabricate arose, and Holman, whose own fault was at issue, already had an interest in explaining the collision favorably when he made them.

The brief notes that the burden rule, the conflict characterization and the Rule 51 formulation are historical features of this 1959 decision, and that the casebook excerpt concentrates on the Rule 51 preservation issue.

The Second Circuit affirmed. The brief's citation line records that certiorari was denied in 1961.

CP-013:
Mitchell sued Neff in an Oregon state circuit court for attorney services. Neff was not an Oregon resident when the action began or when judgment was entered, was not personally served, and did not appear. Service was constructive, by newspaper publication. In February 1866 the court entered a default judgment for less than $300 including costs.

Oregon law allowed publication against an absent nonresident having property in the state and separately allowed attachment in money actions. The land at issue was not attached or otherwise brought before the court during Mitchell's suit. It first became connected with the litigation when the sheriff levied execution after judgment. Pennoyer's asserted title depended on the resulting sale.

Neff claimed the land under a federal patent issued in 1866, and the property was alleged to be worth $15,000. This account follows the reported opinion; the casebook's later historical narrative about Mitchell and the chain of purchases is not a judicial finding.

CP-037:
The Court rejected an excessively formal distinction, associated with Hurn v. Oursler, between two grounds supporting a single cause of action and two separate causes of action. The constitutional question concerns the relationship among the facts and claims forming the controversy, not the legal labels the plaintiff selected. The procedural rules did not themselves enlarge jurisdiction; they helped explain why the older approach was unsatisfactory. Here both theories concerned the same confrontation at the mine and the resulting losses, and a substantial federal claim made them a single constitutional case. A federal theory that fails after trial differs from one so insubstantial that it cannot support jurisdiction at the outset.

The Court then separated power from its exercise. A plaintiff has no automatic right to keep every related state claim in federal court. Judicial economy, convenience, fairness, the desirability of letting state courts decide state law, predominance of state issues, and possible jury confusion all bear on the choice. When the federal claims disappear before trial, the state claims ordinarily should be dismissed as well; when substantial litigation has occurred, economy and fairness may favor retention. The judgment is a continuing one throughout the proceedings. Here the theories were tried together, the federal theory reached a jury verdict, and federal preemption closely affected the state claim, so retention was permissible.

The following comes from the full opinion beyond the assigned excerpt. State-law recovery had to be connected to the violence or threats the state could regulate. Under § 6, the representative's efforts to stop violence, his handling of the picket line, and ordinary assistance to strikers did not establish knowing approval of the earlier unlawful acts.

Justice Harlan, joined by Justice Clark, joined Part I and agreed with reversal but considered the broader preemption discussion unnecessary and read § 6 as restricting inferences of union authorization or ratification from ordinary organizational conduct.

CP-038:
The Court began with the need for statutory authority. Gibbs identifies the outer relationship among claims, but district courts still need authorization from Congress. Finley refused to infer authority over claims involving additional parties, and Congress responded in 1990 with § 1367; agreement that Congress reversed Finley did not establish that the statute did only that.

Subsection (a) refers to civil actions within original jurisdiction and then grants supplemental jurisdiction over all other sufficiently related claims. The majority read the first requirement as satisfied by an otherwise qualifying claim; requiring original jurisdiction over every claim would make the supplemental grant largely self-defeating. Subsection (b), in actions founded solely on diversity, withdraws jurisdiction over claims by plaintiffs against parties added under Rules 14, 19, 20, or 24 and claims of persons joining as plaintiffs under Rule 19 or intervening as plaintiffs under Rule 24, where jurisdiction would be inconsistent with § 1332, but makes no corresponding exclusion for Rule 20 plaintiffs or Rule 23 class members. The majority rejected an indivisibility theory, under which every claim stands or falls as one jurisdictional unit, and a contamination theory: a nondiverse opposing party undermines the premise of a neutral forum, but a smaller related claim does not make the qualifying claim less substantial. The different treatment of Rule 19 and Rule 20 plaintiffs was admittedly awkward, but a possible drafting omission did not authorize adding an exception absent from the text. The majority regarded the text as unambiguous and rejected reliance on legislative history, which it also found conflicting. In a part omitted from the assigned excerpt, it held that the Class Action Fairness Act did not resolve these cases.

Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justices Stevens, O'Connor, and Breyer, dissented: subsection (a)'s reference to original jurisdiction incorporated complete diversity and the rule that each plaintiff meet the amount. Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Breyer, dissented, treating the House Report as strong evidence that Congress meant only to overturn Finley while preserving Zahn.

On May 20 the district court ordered the parties to show why it should not return the state claims to state court while keeping the federal claims, and it then remanded all three state claims without explaining which reason supported its decision. The defendants sought mandamus. A January opinion and its dissent were withdrawn and replaced by the revised opinion of May 16, 1994, which the brief addresses. The Ninth Circuit granted the writ and vacated the remand order.

CP-042:
The patent defendants lived and maintained their only place of business in Dallas, where the alleged infringement occurred. Other litigation involving the patents was pending in the Northern District of Illinois, and discovery there had produced evidence potentially useful in this case. The defendants therefore preferred Illinois and offered to waive venue objections and appear there if the action was transferred. The plaintiffs objected because Illinois was not a district in which the defendants resided, maintained a business, infringed the patents, or could originally have been served.

The companion defendants were Indiana corporations doing business in Illinois, but they were not incorporated, licensed, doing business, or amenable to service in Utah. Utah offered practical advantages: corporate officers, records, and many shareholders were there, Utah law governed, and its court's calendar was less congested. Those defendants likewise offered to appear and waive venue objections in Utah. The companion-case details supplement the assigned excerpt. The parties conceded that venue and reach of process were lacking in the proposed districts at the outset.

CP-043:
The Court treated convenience as the central purpose of forum non conveniens. If a plaintiff could defeat dismissal whenever the foreign forum offered less favorable law, the doctrine would provide little relief in the very cases where a plaintiff selected an inconvenient forum for legal advantage, and a single factor would displace the flexible assessment; Canada Malting had allowed dismissal despite a comparable disadvantage. The proposed rule would also require extensive choice-of-law and comparative-law litigation at a preliminary stage. In a part of the full opinion beyond the excerpt, the Court explained that Van Dusen's preservation of applicable law under § 1404(a) concerned transfer within a unified federal system and could not be imported into a common-law dismissal.

The Court preserved a limit: inconvenience cannot justify sending a plaintiff to a forum offering no meaningful remedy. Scottish negligence remedies allowed litigation of the accident, and the defendants' undertakings supported availability. Reduced deference followed from an inference about convenience, which is weaker for foreign beneficiaries represented by a locally appointed administratrix, though a foreign plaintiff's choice still receives some weight.

On private interests, American design and testing records pointed one way and British maintenance, pilot-training, investigation, and damages evidence the other; the district court could reasonably conclude that a Scottish trial would present fewer proof problems. Defendants need not identify every unavailable witness. The inability to implead the owner, operator, and pilot's estate particularly mattered. On public interests, Scotland had a strong local interest, and even assuming American law would govern, the remaining factors supported Scotland. The Third Circuit had substituted its own assessment despite the abuse-of-discretion standard.

Justice White agreed with Parts I and II but would not have decided the balancing issues. Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Brennan, agreed on the law-disadvantage question but would have remanded to the Third Circuit to reconsider whether Pennsylvania was inconvenient.

CP-047:
The first error concerned the opportunity to develop the record. Under the trial judge's interpretation, Byrd had no reason to rebut the defense on a different statutory theory, and correcting the legal premise on appeal could not fairly deprive him of the chance to meet the defense as properly understood. The manager's testimony presented questions of credibility and inference, so the Fourth Circuit went too far in treating the record as conclusively establishing the defense. This part of the opinion is substantially condensed in the assigned excerpt.

On the Erie issue, the Court first asked whether the state allocation formed part of the substantive workers' compensation relationship. The South Carolina precedent relied on cases involving judicial review of the Industrial Commission's jurisdiction, and the Court found no explanation showing that extending that practice to an affirmative defense in a negligence action was intended to define the parties' entitlements. The state immunity itself remained controlling.

The Court then acknowledged York: a judge and a jury might decide a disputed fact differently, so the allocation potentially affected the outcome. But the federal system has its own essential structure, and assigning disputed facts to a jury is part of it, operating under the influence of the Seventh Amendment. The Court relied on Herron, which had protected the federal judge's role against a state rule assigning a matter to the jury. Unlike disregarding a limitations bar, using a jury did not make a different result certain, since federal judges may comment on evidence and order a new trial.

Justice Whittaker agreed that the directed judgment could not stand but thought letting a jury decide the boundary conflicted with York. Justice Frankfurter, joined by Justice Harlan, who also wrote separately, would have affirmed, believing Byrd's counsel had submitted the issue on the existing evidence.

CP-062:
The court agreed with Winsor that a conversion complaint needed an allegation of ownership or possession at the time of the conversion; an earlier description of the deposit as money belonging to the plaintiffs did not supply it.

The complaint also appeared to state a contract demand, and the plaintiffs asked that the references to fraudulent conversion be disregarded. The court refused because the count had been framed with a double aspect: its financial account resembled assumpsit, while its repeated accusations and its prayer for judgment presented conversion. A defendant should be able to identify the legal controversy from the complaint, not wait until trial to learn which of several inconsistent theories the proof would support.

The court relied on the Wisconsin decisions Pierce v. Carey and Supervisors of Kewaunee County v. Decker, which distinguished simplifying the forms of action from leaving the nature of the action uncertain. Abolishing the common-law forms did not allow tort, contract and equity theories to be fused into one uncertain count.

The court also rejected the plaintiffs' reliance on Revised Code of Civil Procedure § 157(2), on arrest in actions involving an attorney's receipt or misuse of money in a fiduciary capacity: there was no allegation of embezzlement or fraudulent misapplication, and the real dispute was over the reasonable value of professional services.

The brief notes that the case illustrates the restrictive theory-of-the-pleading approach under this historical code and does not apply modern federal alternative-pleading rules.

CP-063:
On the first point, the court relied on decisions directing that the whole petition be considered, especially its leading allegations, and favoring a contract construction where the averments leave the choice doubtful. Garrity could therefore waive the tort and seek the fossil's value on an implied promise to pay. That ruling did not establish that any particular defendant actually owed the implied obligation.

On the second point, Garrity argued that the original implied-contract petition tolled the three-year period and that the amendment related back to commencement. The court rejected this even assuming the facts otherwise disclosed a claim against the former regents. A lawsuit naming one defendant does not suspend limitations against another person simply because its allegations could support liability against that person. Before the amendment no action against the former regents was pending, and by the time they were made defendants the bar had attached. The court applied Kansas law, not the later Federal Rule 15. This discussion comes from the full opinion and is omitted from the assigned excerpt.

On the third point, the new board's authority included managing university property, disbursing appropriations, investing or spending designated funds, and executing trusts or obligations committed to the institutions. The court refused to read that administrative authority as making the board or its members liable for a tort committed by the former regents, and waiving the tort and pleading an implied promise could not create such liability. The university and its managing board were state agencies established for education and administration; without express authority permitting suit, and with no corporate powers conferred on the new board, the action could not be maintained. The court did not find that the removal was lawful or that the fossil lacked value.

CP-080:
The majority accepted that both claims arose from one transaction and the same alleged wrongful conduct. Its objection was to the legal interests and damages being combined. Each spouse had a separate personal claim and a separate potential recovery, and neither had a legal interest in the damages due the other. Even spouses injured while sharing a railroad berth would ordinarily have separate personal-injury causes of action. A preexisting legal relationship could support a joint claim where the wrong injured a common legal interest and produced common damage, as with a partnership, but marriage did not supply that common entitlement. The majority distinguished a husband's formal participation in his wife's action and a husband's independent claim for expenses or loss of services.

The court also relied on its earlier refusal to combine a survival claim belonging to an estate with a death claim benefiting statutory beneficiaries, although both could arise from the same wrong and be prosecuted by the same representative. Separate verdicts and judgments would be needed here. In a part of the opinion omitted from the assigned excerpt, the court added that a motion to make the allegations more definite or to state the counts separately would not cure the joinder defect, and that neither spouse's claim was redundant matter to be struck, so demurrer was an appropriate way to raise the misjoinder.

Justice Fraser, dissenting, treated the alleged denial and disparagement of the marital relationship as an injury to the spouses' common legal relationship, comparable to an injury to a partnership. Charles's individual business losses might be removed on a motion to strike, but he would have upheld the circuit court. The holding turns on South Carolina's statute as it then stood and should not be restated as a rule of modern federal permissive joinder.

CP-083:
The Court identified four interests: those of the plaintiff, the defendant, the absentee and the public. The plaintiff's and defendant's interests depended on timing. Before trial, an adequate alternative forum could favor dismissal; after trial, the plaintiffs had an added interest in preserving their judgment and the resources spent. The insurer had not objected to nonjoinder and had an opportunity to litigate the claims against its policy, so its belated position could not by itself justify discarding the adjudication.

As to the absentee, a nonparty is ordinarily not legally bound by the judgment, but may still suffer practical injury. Dutcher might lose access to policy proceeds before defending claims against himself. The Court regarded that risk as limited and avoidable, without accepting the plaintiffs' assertion that Dutcher faced virtually no tort liability. The Third Circuit had confused an adverse interest under the Dead Man Rule with unavoidable prejudice from this judgment. The Court reserved whether Dutcher's failure to intervene could preclude him from later litigating permission.

Relief could protect Dutcher without dismissal: payment could be withheld while the tort claims proceeded, and the claimants represented that they would accept a limitation of their claims to the policy amount. The public interest in efficient adjudication included preserving completed work. Earlier equity cases created no categorical substantive right to dismissal whenever litigation might affect an absentee; indispensability is a conclusion, not an antecedent classification. Outside the casebook's excerpt, the Court also rejected discretionary dismissal in favor of the state suits, which concerned tort liability and agency rather than coverage and did not include the insurer.

CP-085:
Traditional equitable interpleader required competing claims to the same thing, debt or duty; a common source; a disinterested stakeholder; and no independent liability to either claimant. The 1881 amendment to section 386 removed the common-source requirement and relaxed the identity of demands, though it did not authorize combining unrelated debts merely because one stakeholder owed both.

As pleaded, both groups demanded the same contractual royalties. Had the partnership demanded reasonable use value, mesne profits or damages for waste, that would be a different obligation and would not support interpleader. The lease was not an independent liability, because deciding the claimants' dispute would determine the lessees' responsibility; a contrary view would defeat ordinary interpleader by banks, insurers and escrow holders.

On tenant estoppel, the majority construed section 386 liberally to fulfill its remedial purpose. Abolishing the common-source restriction undermined the associated common-law bar on tenant interpleader, and a neutral tenant could recognize the landlord's title while acknowledging another's asserted claim without adopting it. Otherwise the tenant risked forfeiture or double payment, and the rival claimant risked a landlord's later insolvency. The landlord's delay in receiving rent was a real disadvantage, so the tenant had to allege facts showing a reasonable probability of competing demands, not mere pretext or suspicion; it need not profess uncertainty about who would prevail.

Justice Carter, dissenting in a writing omitted from the casebook excerpt, viewed interpleading the landlord with a claimant of antecedent adverse title as a denial of the landlord's title contrary to section 1962(4), which section 386 did not repeal. He stressed the cost of impounding rent and would have required the adverse claimant to seek an injunction or receiver and furnish security.

CP-088:
Hansen had no continuing official or individual interest: the decree did not bind him after he left office, and injury to his reputation was not an interest the appeal could protect. Smuck had no appealable interest separate from his board membership, since the decree ran against the collective board and being a named defendant at trial did not create a distinct interest in overturning the institutional decision.

On the parents, Bazelon's Part I read Rule 24(a)(2), as amended in 1966, to require an interest related to the transaction, practical impairment, and inadequate representation. The interest requirement was a practical guide; an educational interest could qualify without a financial stake, though the requirement remained a prerequisite. The parents' interest was preserving the board's constitutionally permissible policy discretion. Once the decree became final they might be unable to challenge compliant policies in a new suit, because a policy can be constitutionally permissible without being constitutionally required. The board represented all parents and could weigh publicity, expense and delay differently, so there was a sufficiently serious possibility of inadequate representation on appeal, without any accusation of bad faith. Failure to appeal was a relevant factor, not a universal license to intervene.

Beyond the casebook's excerpt, four judges in Parts II and III rejected a three-judge-court objection and a recusal challenge and sustained the provisions on optional zones, faculty integration and transportation. Part IV treated long-range planning and abolition of the track system as it then operated as not materially limiting the discretion the parents sought to protect.

McGowan would have dismissed all appeals because the choice whether to appeal belonged to the board, but joined the dispositions to resolve the case. Danaher, joined by Burger and Tamm, dissented and would have vacated the decree and left matters to the elected board; Burger, joined by Tamm, separately dissented, stressing judicial limits in educational policy.

CP-090:
The majority required a connection among the reasons for the challenged decisions, which a common biased test or significant proof of a general discriminatory policy might supply. Here the employer formally prohibited sex discrimination and the plaintiffs showed no companywide method of exercising the delegated discretion. The majority recognized that discretionary systems can violate Title VII; its conclusion was about whether this evidence supported adjudicating all the claims together.

Bielby's testimony showed susceptibility to bias but did not estimate how often stereotypes actually affected decisions, so it was inadequate even assuming it was admissible; the majority questioned the district court's refusal to apply Daubert at certification without resolving that point. National and regional statistics did not establish a shared cause of decisions at individual stores, and the anecdotes were too limited and geographically uneven to prove a companywide policy. The majority denied importing Rule 23(b)(3) predominance: differences among employees mattered because they defeated the proposed common answer.

In Part III of the full opinion, which the casebook's excerpt omits, the Court explained that Rule 23(b)(2) concerns an indivisible injunction or declaration benefiting the class as a whole. Individualized monetary claims need the protections of Rule 23(b)(3), including predominance, superiority, notice and the chance to opt out. The Court reserved whether genuinely incidental monetary relief could ever be included. Title VII entitled Wal-Mart to present individual defenses to backpay claims, and the Rules Enabling Act barred replacing those proceedings with extrapolation from a sample.

Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justices Breyer, Sotomayor and Kagan, agreed with the Rule 23(b)(2) holding but dissented from Part II. She viewed the common discretionary pay and promotion system, reinforced by corporate culture, as presenting a disputed issue that could advance all claims, and would have let the district court consider Rule 23(b)(3) on remand.

CP-091:
Consolidated actions asserted state-law claims in eleven states. The district court partly granted certification, establishing eleven damages classes under Rule 23(b)(3). It required an objective class definition based on purchases during the class period but declined to demand an additional administratively feasible method of identifying members. ConAgra obtained interlocutory review under Rule 23(f).

On January 3, 2017, the Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court's refusal to condition certification on the extra identification showing. A footnote states that ConAgra's other challenges to certification were addressed in a concurrently filed memorandum disposition; the full brief covers only the published opinion and has not analyzed that memorandum.

CP-095:
The 2015 amendment to Rule 26(b)(1) placed proportionality in the operative definition of the scope of discovery. The court treated that requirement as demanding a practical relationship between the likely informational value of requested material and the burden and expense of producing it. In product-design discovery, similarity is therefore not all-or-nothing. Functional similarity, common testing standards, interchangeability and knowledgeable technical testimony can support discovery beyond the precise model involved in the accident, while declining similarity reduces the justification for broad production.

The court distinguished ordinary design and testing information from prior-accident or litigation files. Evidence of prior incidents used to show notice or defect depends more heavily on substantial similarity of circumstances, so broad production about materially different caps or systems was unwarranted. The court limited the time period by reference to when the relevant products were manufactured and sold, not mechanically from the date of injury.

Applying these distinctions, the court held warranty and testing information on open, screw, covered and duckbill caps discoverable, subject to work-product protection, but excluded prior-claim files on the three alternative designs because the plaintiffs had not established substantial similarity of the accidents. Mower discovery was confined to the Simplicity Axion, Snapper 150Z, Craftsman ZT7000, Craftsman ZT75000 and Coronet. The court rejected the request for settlement releases and related communications under Evidence Rule 408, allowed specified claims-review records, required sufficiently specific privilege logs, and set January 1, 2000, about five years before manufacture, as the earliest discovery date. These were discovery rulings only; the court stressed that discovery breadth does not decide admissibility or liability. The brief adds that a component can be similar enough for discovery without qualifying as a feasible alternative design or proving defect.

CP-101:
Federal Rule of Evidence 501 directs courts to develop privilege principles through reason and experience. The privilege serves legal advice by encouraging complete and candid communication, and effective advice requires factual information delivered to counsel as well as instructions delivered to decisionmakers. Limiting the former to senior management defeats that function in a corporation, where the employees who know what happened often have no authority over the legal response. Employees below the management group had taken part in the questioned transactions, and those outside senior management may also implement the advice. The control-group test was also unpredictably applied.

To the Sixth Circuit's fear that a broader privilege would conceal misconduct, the Court answered by distinguishing facts from communications about facts. The IRS could ask an employee what payments were made, to whom and why, but could not compel the employee's confidential report to counsel or counsel's record of it. Upjohn had supplied witness lists and the IRS had conducted interviews; convenience did not defeat the privilege. The Court declined to lay down rules for every investigation and expressly reserved whether the privilege covers former employees.

On work product, nothing in the summons statute showed that Congress meant to eliminate the protection recognized in Hickman, and Rule 26(b)(3) incorporated work-product safeguards; the Government conceded that the Sixth Circuit's categorical exclusion was wrong. Counsel's notes reveal mental impressions through selection, phrasing and evaluation, and Rule 26(b)(3) separately protects mental impressions, conclusions, opinions and legal theories. The magistrate applied only the ordinary substantial-need and undue-hardship standard, so the remaining claim was remanded.

Chief Justice Burger, concurring in part and in the judgment, would have stated a clear minimum rule protecting communications by an employee or former employee, at management's direction, with authorized counsel about conduct within the employment. The assigned excerpt omits his opinion.

CP-106:
The Court first separated power from necessity. If nonconsensual assistance of this kind could lawfully be used at all, the hundreds of entries, changing prices and disputed allowances amply justified the district court's view that an auditor was needed. The auditor could isolate the genuine disagreements and so reduce what the jury had to resolve.

An auditor's assessment of conflicting testimony did not make the appointment an unconstitutional substitute for trial. Although the report might suffice as evidence unless challenged, its conclusions were tentative, the order reserved the ultimate facts to the jury, and the parties could introduce their own proof and challenge the other side's. The Court acknowledged that this form of auditor was not an established feature of English or colonial jury practice before the Constitution; the closest model developed in Massachusetts after 1818. But the Seventh Amendment preserves the jury right without freezing every rule of pleading, evidence or trial preparation, and new procedures are permissible if they do not obstruct the right or interfere with the jury's ultimate factual authority. A rule may give an official finding rebuttable evidentiary status without binding the jury.

Because no act of Congress expressly authorized the appointment, the Court turned to inherent authority. Courts had long appointed masters, examiners and similar assistants in equity, and the same need could arise in an action at law. A compulsory reference that finally determined the disputed facts, by contrast, would interfere with the jury right.

On expenses, Congress had provided no public funding, and necessary court-ordered litigation expenses had historically been treated as taxable costs. In actions at law, however, federal practice entitled the prevailing party to taxable costs as a rule, without the flexibility of equity, so the allocation clause was wrong. The decision predates the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, and the assigned excerpt omits the costs discussion.

CP-108:
The plaintiffs could proceed in Coulas's absence but still had to prove their claims, and the judgment that resulted from that hearing lay outside Rule 55(b)'s notice requirement. Calling the event a default in a minute entry did not change its legal character. The court relied on Bass v. Hoagland and Klein v. Rappaport, both of which distinguish a pleading default from nonattendance after the case is at issue. The phrase otherwise defend covers preliminary defensive steps, such as jurisdictional attacks or motions, that prevent default without an answer; it does not require a party who has answered to be present at every trial call to avoid confessing the complaint.

In a part of the opinion omitted from the assigned excerpt, the court addressed Phoenix Metals Corp. v. Roth, on which Coulas relied for the statement that notice is required before a default judgment against a party who has answered. That case involved an answer mistakenly attached to the wrong file. To the extent its language suggested that default was appropriate after an answer on the merits, the court called the implication incorrect; the proper route is proof and a merits judgment.

Coulas's objection to the stipulation resetting trial failed because setting trial is the court's function under Rule 40, and he had an opportunity to object to the court's order. His claim of missing notice lacked support in the minutes, and the court presumed that the clerk performed the duty to notify under Rule 77(h) absent a contrary showing; attending on the original date would also have revealed the change. The court did not treat an actual failure of notice, adequately shown on another record, as categorically immaterial. The conclusions arise under the Arizona rules as they stood in 1964.

CP-112:
Patent-infringement actions seeking legal relief descended from actions tried at law, and their jury character was undisputed. The distinct question was the subsidiary task of claim construction; protecting the substance of the jury right does not require assigning every step in a legal action to the jury.

Modern claim practice lacked an eighteenth-century counterpart, so the Court examined specification construction as the closest historical practice. The surviving cases did not establish that juries construed disputed patent terms; judges ordinarily construed written instruments. Markman's argument about terms of art rested on nineteenth-century statements that did not establish a controlling practice at the founding. The Court left open whether its treatment of technical terms should extend to other written instruments.

Precedent reinforced the allocation: Winans v. Denmead had separated judicial construction from the jury's determination of infringement, and Souter distinguished Bischoff v. Wethered and Tucker v. Spalding as cases using evidence to understand the accused things. The need for expert testimony did not make interpretation a jury function, because a proposed meaning still had to fit the patent as a whole, and the Court expected most credibility judgments to be embedded in that evaluation. Uniformity was a further reason: judicial construction permits precedential reasoning and appellate supervision, while issue preclusion would not bind new defendants. The Court did not promise complete uniformity.

CP-113:
A preference rises to disqualifying bias when it naturally implies that the juror would not act impartially, and prejudice means prejudgment. Schmidt's categorical views about drinking, coupled with her statements about the family, showed that she had prejudged matters central to parental fitness, so the record established statutory disqualification as a matter of law. Alternatively, even if bias had remained a factual question for the trial judge, her established views could not be erased by agreeing to a leading assurance that she could decide on the evidence, and retaining her was an abuse of discretion. The opinion's footnote explains that the cited law required disregarding a biased juror's assurance of being able to put bias aside. The court also stated that a complainant need not independently establish probable injury from juror disqualification, though it found supporting harm in the evidence about peremptory-challenge choices.

The complete opinion addressed other errors. The mother bore the burden on whether she was a fit custodian, yet was denied the right to open and close argument that Rules 266 and 269 ordinarily gave the party bearing the burden. The judge also refused to hear divorce evidence after the custody verdict despite having reserved that issue. The court viewed the accumulated errors as requiring a new trial and emphasized that the custody verdict was binding under the statute then applicable.

CP-119:
Legal components of mixed questions received plenary review and factual components clear-error review. Rule 52(a) expressly permitted findings stated orally and recorded in open court after the evidence closed, and prompt findings promoted speedy adjudication and used the judge's fresh recollection, although a carefully prepared written opinion might often be preferable. Under Anderson v. Bessemer City, adopted findings are still those of the judge. The record showed informed, considered views, and the court reserved that it might view a different record differently. A footnote rejected reliance on Roberts v. Ross as superseded by Anderson and the circuit's Hayes decision.

On groundwater, where two views of the evidence were permissible the trial court's choice was not clearly erroneous, and the Authority bore the burden of proving the threatened contamination.

Monitoring expenses could be recoverable even without actual contamination, so the failure to prove a continuing threat did not dispose of them. CP-133:
Interore sold 22,202 metric tons of fertilizer to East Coast Fertilizer in New Zealand for $4,118,287, including cost and freight. It chartered the vessel Adelina and engaged SGS to inspect the holds and certify their suitability. The vessel had carried coal immediately before and barley before that; cleaning and painting left barley behind structural stringers. A Swedish SGS affiliate inspected two holds. SGS's Tampa inspector spent about half an hour on the other three, walking through without looking behind the stringers; he later learned of the earlier cargoes but did not return. SGS issued a certificate of readiness and charged $150 for the Tampa inspection.

In New Zealand, authorities found barley contamination and would permit unloading only if buyers were informed and restrictions protected barley-growing areas. East Coast refused the shipment. After efforts to find other buyers failed, Interore sent the fertilizer to Antwerp and sold it in smaller lots, incurring additional expense and losses. SGS neither owned the vessel nor undertook the transportation; the brief notes that the casebook editors' bracketed introduction inaccurately describes SGS as transporter and shipowner.

The court first rejected the city's objections to the writ. Removal of the remand did not prevent a constitutional challenge to the power exercised; rehearing was Corcoran's first opportunity to know that the Appellate Court would reverse for factual error under this provision; and the state constitution independently supplied Supreme Court review where statutory validity was involved.

On the merits, the court traced Illinois practice to an 1837 enactment allowing exceptions to denials of new trials and appellate assignments of error based on those rulings. Earlier decisions had reversed verdicts manifestly against the evidence, and the modern provision substantially continued that practice. Cases invalidating a different power, appellate substitution of contrary findings followed by final reversal without remand, did not control; Corcoran's own request, not the statute, had removed the remand.

Because the guarantee preserved jury trial as historically understood, the court examined common-law practice. A judge at nisi prius tried the case and returned the verdict to the court at Westminster, whose judges could grant a new trial on the record without having heard the witnesses. The mechanism let another jury reconsider the dispute rather than making reviewing judges the final factfinders.

That justification required restraint. Slight differences in the balance of testimony were insufficient; precedents required a clearly wrong verdict, a strong preponderance of contrary evidence, or circumstances in which justice demanded intervention. Unrestricted appellate substitution would itself deprive parties of jury trial. The court identified two connected questions. On the first, the track owner acted through Thoroughbred, which acted through the individual employees. Because the corporate liability alleged depended on those agents' actionable wrongdoing, the principals stood or fell with them. The opinion applied this to the specific respondeat-superior claim rather than declaring that every employer and employee share preclusion for all disputes.

On the second, a claim consists of the facts of an occurrence or transaction rather than the legal theory selected. Although the events were nearly a week apart, the removal was the subject of the disorderly-conduct trial and the events were sufficiently interconnected to form one claim. The witnesses to the removal gave the same account whether it was called assault or false arrest, and the employees' statements were the same whether the theory was libel or malicious prosecution. A litigant cannot reserve alternative grounds for recovery from the same alleged invasion and try them serially after losing. Preclusion reached issues tried and others that could have been raised within the claim.

The court also relied on the earlier actual findings, describing Mathews as estopped both directly and collaterally. His pro se status did not require another trial; the court acknowledged the lack of counsel but emphasized that fair adjudication must eventually end litigation. The court first rejected the procedural challenge. The plea raised legal questions that could dispose of the whole action, so a separate hearing was within the judge's statutory discretion; an automatic stay would undermine that sequencing, and Mitchell could still challenge the order on appeal from final judgment.

On preclusion, the governing principle requires the holder of an entire, indivisible demand to present its whole scope rather than litigate piecemeal, and it applies to use of a claim as a setoff or defense as well as to successive plaintiff's suits. Mitchell's alleged injury was the failure to account for approximately $18,000 in crop proceeds, one demand against the bank. When the bank sued for approximately $9,000, he could invoke that demand defensively or seek affirmative judgment for the balance. Having chosen the defensive use and gained the benefit of defeating the notes, he could not later enforce the remainder. In Kirven the earlier defendant had withdrawn the defense before later suing; Ludlow involved uncertain pleadings and possible innocent lack of knowledge. The court recognized exceptions such as a court's own limitation of recovery or lack of knowledge, and found none here. Cases from other jurisdictions applied the same principle; winning on the defense creates no exception.

CP-141:
The Court accepted that a question directly determined by a competent court cannot be litigated again between the same parties. The obstacle was evidentiary: a judgment establishes a result but may not identify each issue essential to it, so the party asserting estoppel must connect the proposition asserted to a necessary determination in the first case.

Sometimes the record makes the connection evident. When it does not, extrinsic evidence may explain what was submitted and necessarily decided, but it must be consistent with the record and cannot enlarge the adjudication by showing that another issue could have been raised. The Sickles litigation illustrated the point: a general verdict on several counts might rest on ordinary money claims rather than the special contract later said to be settled.

Russell's record had the same defect. The declaration alleged infringement generally without saying whether the unlawful act was use of fat liquor itself or use of the particular patented process, and the jury could have found for Russell under either claim. Because a patent can be valid as to one claim and invalid as to another, a verdict supporting one did not necessarily reject every defense directed at the other. With no extrinsic evidence, the Court could only conjecture, and conjecture was insufficient for estoppel. Because the second suit addressed subsequent conduct, the precise adjudicated question had to be shown, not every defense that could have been offered earlier.

The report records that Justice Clifford dissented but gives no reasoning. The brief notes that, read with Cromwell, the case adds an identification requirement to issue preclusion.

CP-144:
Judge Staton explained that a consent judgment has a dual character: it embodies an agreement and also invokes judicial authority. A judgment-centered approach stresses finality, avoidance of harassment and conservation of resources. An agreement-centered approach asks what the parties actually settled; requiring settlement of every possible issue could deter compromise because a party might inadvertently surrender something. After considering divergent federal decisions and distinguishing Indiana cases attacking the validity of earlier consent judgments, the court adopted the agreement-centered approach, noting that Rule 68's structure also allows settlement of part of a controversy.

That approach did not make Anderson's private intention controlling. Both parties had to agree, and the reserved matter had to be precise. The court required that the reservation be incorporated into the offer of judgment itself and that the reserved claim be an inherent part of the original complaint. The complaint here asked for specific performance or profits over the lease term; it stated no claim for profits lost during delayed delivery, and the acceptance's general reference to breach damages did not show Hanover's assent to that residual claim.

The court's notes extend the reservation requirement to an issue or another cause of action, not just damages, and bar curing the deficiency by later amendment: the claim had to be in the complaint when the parties agreed and the consent judgment was entered. Judge Hoffman concurred on the authority of General Discount Corp. v. Weiss Machinery without a developed alternative analysis. The casebook excerpt omits the qualification that judgment had not actually been entered.

Justice Traynor separated two questions the traditional formula combined: who may assert a judgment and against whom it may operate. No one can lose rights through a judgment without the notice and opportunity to participate that due process requires, so the person against whom preclusion is invoked must have been a party or privy. But another person's absence from the first litigation does not erase the first party's fair adjudication, and a litigant who has had the opportunity to contest an issue should not reopen it merely by choosing another adversary. Existing exceptions for derivative liability, such as principal and agent or employer and servant, already reflected that reasoning despite the absence of mutuality.

Bernhard's change from objecting beneficiary to administratrix did not change the right represented, since in both capacities recovery was sought for the estate's legatees and creditors. An intervening California decision established the probate court's jurisdiction despite Cook's resignation. The court did not retry whether Sather made a valid gift.

The majority began with the ordinary limit on a judgment's reach: a litigant is entitled to a hearing on his own rights, and a decree binding its parties does not dispose of an outsider's separate federal claim.

The petitioners proposed a duty to intervene when a person knew or should have known that pending litigation might affect his interests. The Court found no such duty in Rule 24, which makes intervention available, not compulsory; appearing as an amicus or having a chance to object differs from being a party. Rule 19 addresses persons whose interests may be affected, and the parties negotiating a decree know the relief sought and are positioned to identify those they wish to bind. A mandatory-intervention rule would force outsiders to monitor litigation and would generate later disputes over notice and foreseeability, shifting burdens to those less informed. The value of settling complex employment disputes did not let the original parties settle claims they did not own. The Court preserved exceptions for representative proceedings and special statutory schemes. The decree defendants could still contest the later claims on the merits; decree compliance could not automatically replace that inquiry.

The court applied the New York Court of Appeals' recent Schwartz formulation: an identical issue must have been necessarily decided and be decisive in the current action, and the party to be bound must have had a full and fair opportunity to contest it. The airline's liability for the crash met the identity requirement, and the court viewed a common airplane-crash liability question as lacking the participant-specific complications of a multi-vehicle collision. The airline bore the burden of showing it lacked a full opportunity in the nineteen-day Texas trial and did not meet it.

Justice Frank distinguished the earlier Hart ruling because these plaintiffs and their decedents were New York domiciliaries. In his interest analysis, New York had the superior interest in the preclusion question affecting its own residents, and Texas had no legitimate interest in imposing its restrictive preclusion rule on them. CP-ATLAS-ORTIZ:
A limited-fund class binds claimants who cannot all recover in full from one inadequate resource, and because it is mandatory, absent members lack the opt-out right of Rule 23(b)(3). The traditional cases shared three characteristics: definite maximums for the claims and the fund showing insufficiency; the whole inadequate fund devoted to the claims; and inclusion and equitable treatment of claimants sharing the recovery theory. These were presumptively necessary, and a proponent departing from them had to justify it. The Rule's history, the Rules Enabling Act, and jury-trial and due-process concerns supported caution, though the Court did not hold every mandatory limited-fund settlement unconstitutional.

Applying this, an agreed payment figure shows what parties will pay, not the maximum available; the district court needed an independent evidentiary basis for the limit and insufficiency, and a later fairness hearing could not substitute. Settlement value might be evidence after disinterested bargaining, but class counsel also represented inventory clients whose payments depended on a global deal. The Court did not find the policies sufficient to pay everyone; it held insufficiency unproven.

A mandatory class should include the competing claims on the fund, yet the inventory and pending claimants were outside it and appeared to receive better terms. Within the class, present and future claimants, and those exposed before and after Continental's policy expired in 1959, had conflicting interests requiring homogeneous subclasses with separate representation; a Rule 23(e) fairness review could not swallow Rule 23(a)'s adequacy requirement.

Rehnquist, concurring with Scalia and Kennedy, said the asbestos crisis called for legislation. Breyer, dissenting with Stevens, would have deferred to the district court's findings and treated the disputed insurance asset as a genuine limited fund. The casebook's assigned excerpt substantially compresses the majority.

CP-ATLAS-TRANSUNION:
Standing requires a concrete, particularized, actual or imminent injury, caused by the defendant and redressable by the court. Tangible harm readily qualifies; intangible harm can qualify through a close relationship to a harm traditionally recognized as a basis for suit, such as reputational injury, though an exact historical duplicate is unnecessary. Congress's identification of harms deserves respect, but a statutory cause of action does not itself eliminate the requirement of concrete injury, a limit the majority grounded in separation of powers. Standing must exist for each claim and form of relief, with proof appropriate to the stage of litigation.

Publication of misleading alerts to third-party businesses harmed the 1,853 members in a way closely related to defamation; labeling someone a potential terrorist was sufficiently analogous to falsely labeling the person a terrorist. For the remaining members, inaccurate information in an internal file resembled a defamatory letter stored in a drawer. A sufficiently imminent and substantial risk can support an injunction, but an unmaterialized risk alone does not support retrospective damages absent a separate concrete injury, and there was no proof the undistributed alerts were later disseminated. On the mailing claims, there was no evidence that anyone besides Ramirez opened the letters, was confused or distressed, or would have acted differently.

Justice Thomas, joined by Justices Breyer, Sotomayor, and Kagan, dissented. In his historical account, violation of a private right owed to a specific individual supported suit without proof of additional loss; each duty here ran to a specific consumer, and he also argued the harms satisfied the majority's own test. Justice Kagan, joined by Justices Breyer and Sotomayor, agreed with his result but retained the concrete-injury requirement, deferring to Congress's judgment about real harms and risks except in highly unusual cases.

The casebook treats the case in an editorial note, not a full judicial excerpt.

A jury returned a $2,000 verdict for the plaintiff. After an unsuccessful motion for a new trial, the defendant appealed to the St. Louis Court of Appeals. The appeal did not challenge the sufficiency of the plaintiff's evidence to reach the jury. On December 20, 1949 the court reversed the judgment and remanded the cause. A motion for rehearing or transfer was denied on January 20, 1950.

Under the court's stated Missouri doctrine, an injury neither pleaded nor necessarily resulting from a pleaded injury is an item of special damage requiring its own specific statement. The petition alleged no injury from which increased blood pressure could be regarded as inevitable, and the evidence did not establish inevitability; the same problem applied to the shoulder injury.

The court acknowledged that the defendant could not fairly claim surprise, but distinguished absence of surprise from satisfaction of the statutory pleading requirement. The defendant was entitled to insist that special damages appear in the petition, and the plaintiff had not sought to amend, though amendment could have been sought on appropriate terms.

The plaintiff invoked Missouri's liberalized Civil Code, including sections 35, 36, and 57. The court read those provisions together with section 52, which expressly required specific statement of special damages; general liberalization could not nullify that specific requirement. Her reliance on federal Form 10 and on the code's kinship with the Federal Rules was likewise subordinate to section 52.

The defendant did not waive its objection by offering its own blood-pressure evidence, because it objected consistently and responded only after its objections were overruled. The court held the error prejudicial on this record; it did not say every pleading defect requires reversal. It rejected a separate challenge to instructions 1 and 2 and did not reach the challenge to instruction 8.

In the casebook's excerpt of the rehearing opinion, the plaintiff argued that the Missouri language was copied from Federal Rule 9(g); Judge McCullen answered that the plain language does not permit pleading only general damages and recovering special damages. The casebook substitutes a bracketed reference to Missouri Rule 55.19, an editorial modernization, and its five notes are editorial teaching material.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-064:
The Court rejected the attempt to make an ordinary debt's original location decisive. An obligation to pay was enforceable against the debtor wherever he could be sued and did not become unenforceable because he crossed a state boundary for a short visit. Unlike a tangible object, a debt could not be physically seized; garnishment arrested the obligation through notice to the debtor and a direction not to pay his original creditor.

Maryland satisfied both parts of the test. Balk could have sued Harris there despite their shared North Carolina residence, which the Court connected to the privileges and immunities of citizens of the several states. Maryland's attachment provisions covered credits in another person's hands, and personal service supplied power over Harris. The attaching creditor was treated as representing the garnishee's creditor in reaching an obligation the latter could himself enforce in Maryland.

Harris admittedly owed the debt and had no defense to condemnation once jurisdiction was acquired, so consenting to the judgment Epstein was entitled to obtain did not strip the payment of its protective effect.

The Court added a qualification. A garnishee owes his own creditor notice so that the creditor can contest the attaching claim, and negligently failing to give it could prevent the garnishee from relying on the judgment and payment. On this record Balk learned of the judgment promptly, had a year and a day to challenge it, and did not, so there was no basis to deny Harris the judgment's protection.

The casebook calls the notice discussion dictum; the brief notes that the opinion develops the qualification and applies it to the facts. The brief explains the historical decision without certifying its rule as current law.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-074:
A cause of action for an unpaid bill was intangible property, and the statute extinguished it when no timely claim was filed. It did not matter that the notice invited participation rather than announcing a merits hearing; a proceeding could adversely affect an interest without resolving its validity.

On state action, the majority accepted that mere adoption of an ordinary limitation period does not generally create a duty to notify every potential claimant, and accepted the executrix's reading of Texaco v. Short, but rejected her characterization of this statute as self-executing. The deadline did not run simply because time elapsed after death: probate had to begin, the court had to appoint an executor or executrix, the court ordered notice, and proof of publication was filed with it. The court's involvement activated and permeated the process that terminated the claim.

Applying Mullane and Mennonite, the Court balanced effective notice against prompt estate administration. Creditors might not know of the death or of probate, an executor with a beneficial interest might lack incentive to call attention to claims, and publication was a poor way of reaching them. The state's interest in swift settlement was accommodated by a bounded duty: reasonably diligent efforts to identify creditors, then inexpensive mailed notice. Impracticable searches and notice to those with merely conjectural claims were not required.

Chief Justice Rehnquist found the distinction from Texaco unpersuasive: in both, state law prescribed a time bar that courts later applied, and probate's routine administrative steps were perfunctory.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-075:
An opportunity to defend has little value if a person does not know proceedings are pending, so Mullane requires notice reasonably calculated, in the circumstances, to apprise interested parties and permit objections. Personal service is ideal but not universally required; the question was whether the substitute met the constitutional minimum.

The officials argued that eviction was an in rem proceeding that could be commenced by notice posted on the property. Justice Brennan refused to decide adequacy by assigning an in rem or in personam label. Losing continued residence in one's home was a significant deprivation even when possession was the only remedy sought.

Dusenbery urged the three-factor Mathews test. Chief Justice Rehnquist chose Mullane, explaining that Mathews was not an all-purpose formula for every procedural due process question and that the Court regularly used Mullane to assess how notice was given. The majority distinguished direct notice as a method from actual notice as receipt. Earlier decisions accepting mail did not make proof of receipt indispensable, and Mennonite was read as requiring efforts to provide actual notice, not a guaranteed outcome. Federal custody did not require extraordinary measures. Dusenbery proposed that an employee watch him open the notice and obtain a signed receipt; the majority regarded that mainly as a means of proving receipt, which the Constitution did not require, and stressed the difficulty of reconstructing delivery years later and the resulting uncertainty in property titles. It found no probative record evidence that a signature system materially improved delivery itself. The government's later improvement of its procedures did not prove the earlier system unconstitutional.

Justice Ginsburg agreed that Mullane governed but focused on the link from prison staff to a prisoner whose location the government controlled. Unlike the beneficiaries in Mullane, Dusenbery's claim stood alone. She proposed a feasible safeguard, an inmate signature or documented refusal as later prison procedures required, rather than an unconditional actual-receipt requirement.

Whether a judgment is void under Rule 60(b)(4) is a question of law, not of discretion, and a party attacking a void judgment need not first show a meritorious defense, though the Aguchaks bore the burden of establishing the defect.

Small-claims rules already permitted a written statement of the defense, and Alaska law required a change of venue in specified circumstances of unnecessary expense and inconvenience. Given the prohibitive travel burden, the court expected a transfer if there was a reasonable prospect of a defense requiring a hearing. Although failing to request a venue change ordinarily waives the objection, the challenge here was to a form that left the couple unaware of the written option.

Applying Mullane's requirement of notice reasonably calculated to inform and permit objections, the court looked to the recipients' circumstances. Collection defendants commonly lack counsel and legal sophistication, and remoteness made that worse. A command to travel hundreds of miles at substantial cost, with no practicable alternative identified, could communicate that defense was unavailable. The court drew a limited analogy to notice sent to a known incompetent, without calling the Aguchaks incompetent.

Correcting the form imposed little burden. The court acknowledged the State's interest in an efficient credit economy, but explaining existing procedures added no defenses, and the interest in keeping the form was essentially avoiding reprinting costs.

The court could not affirm merely because Khashoggi knew of the proceeding, since actual notice does not cure void service. A footnote observed that a February 1989 letter from his criminal lawyer undermined his claimed lack of knowledge, but that skepticism was no substitute for compliance with the rule.

Reading the rule to allow only one home would fit poorly with a person who permanently maintains several residences and travels among them. Citizenship or domicile did not require the court to ignore where Khashoggi actually lived. The court examined conflicting state and federal authorities without trying to settle every variation of multi-residence service and decided the facts before it.

Two features together supported the result. Olympic Tower was permanently maintained as his home, shown by ownership, furnishing, remodeling and his later identification of it as a residence. And he was actually living there when the housekeeper received the papers. Under Mullane's reasonable-notice principle, delivery there to a resident housekeeper was reasonably calculated to alert him to the action. That reasoning validated this form of service; it did not revive the proposition that any defective method becomes valid when notice arrives. The court announced no minimum value, size or staff for abode service.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-085:
The statute aims to give the corporation notice that litigation has begun and is to be liberally construed; its history expanded the kinds of corporate recipients rather than confining service to a few titles. Zurich argued that appointment required express authority and a written, acknowledged, filed designation under CPLR 318. The majority rejected that reading and did not need to decide that every executive secretary is a managing agent.

A corporation can set up procedures in which a receptionist directs servers to a secretary who forwards legal papers, but it cannot use those procedures and then escape their consequences by pointing to title or the lack of a filed designation. Servers generally cannot know a company's private allocation of responsibilities.

The rule is qualified. Delivery to a building receptionist who is not the defendant's employee, without inquiry, would fail even if she forwarded the papers, and not every employee's claim to represent the corporation is a reasonable basis for service. Later actual notice alone does not cure careless delivery.

Here the server went to Zurich's own offices, announced his purpose, asked whom to see, followed directions, and obtained Robertson's confirmation. Both employees were longstanding staff of an insurer regularly involved in litigation. If they directed him to the wrong person, the error was Zurich's.

Judge Gabrielli agreed that Robertson had been impliedly appointed to receive process, which sufficed under CPLR 311, but objected to the emphasis on the server's reasonableness or diligence. In his view the legislature prescribed eligible recipients, reviving failed service because the attempt was reasonable could encourage sloppy practice, and any exception should rest on the corporation's obstruction or estoppel.

The casebook cites the case for Robertson's established practice and corporate routing procedures; the brief notes that the casebook attributes the agent-by-appointment formulation to the Court of Appeals, although that was the Appellate Division's ground.

The United States filed the action in the Southern District of New York, invoking 28 U.S.C. § 1345, which gives district courts jurisdiction over civil actions commenced by the United States. The defendants moved under Rule 12 to dismiss, for a more definite statement, and to strike. District Judge Frankel denied the motions in all respects; the requests to clarify or strike were denied without prejudice to similar contentions in discovery or pretrial proceedings. With the government's acquiescence, he recognized a controlling legal question with grounds for interlocutory appeal under § 1292(b). The casebook reports a later settlement.

Judge Frankel began with In re Debs, which allowed the United States to seek judicial relief against obstruction of interstate rail transportation and the mails. Debs did not confine the government's standing to proprietary loss; its reasoning let the government seek help against public wrongs affecting matters constitutionally entrusted to national authority, and later cases applied it in other settings. A suit brought only for a third party's benefit, with no public obligation, would not qualify, but the alleged scale and public effect of the scheme met that limit.

The complaint alleged a substantial burden on commerce through widespread garnishment, and a congressional finding in the Consumer Credit Protection Act linked garnishment with job loss and disruption of employment, production and consumption. Whether the government could prove the effect remained open; at the pleading stage the allegation was accepted. Distinctions between physical and nonphysical obstruction, or direct and indirect effects, did not justify dismissal, though an evidentiary record might show effects too attenuated to suffice.

On the danger of setting federal resources against private defendants, the judge reasoned that Congress could control executive abuses and the court would evaluate the propriety and scope of any relief.

On the alternative ground, he acknowledged that the government's nonstatutory authority was an open question with contrary opinions, but saw no persuasive constitutional distinction between protecting against large-scale burdens on commerce and large-scale denials of due process. Congress's failure to provide this exact authorization did not amount to a prohibition.

The casebook uses the case in its Note on "sewer" service and separately reports a 1972 settlement and consent decree; the brief states that a primary copy of that decree was not recovered and its terms are not independently verified.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-117:
Most limitation periods protect a defendant from stale claims; they are affirmative defenses that can be forfeited or waived and often permit equitable tolling. Other deadlines serve broader systemic interests, such as defining the scope of the Government's consent to suit or promoting judicial efficiency, and the Court sometimes calls these more absolute limitations jurisdictional.

Older cases had placed this statute in the second group. Kendall refused to add an equitable exception to a predecessor six-year statute and required courts to raise timeliness whether or not a party pleaded it; Finn applied the deadline despite a Government agency's voluntary referral of the claim; and Soriano later retained that reading. The 1948 change from claims cognizable by the Court of Claims to claims of which it has jurisdiction made no substantive difference.

Irwin's rebuttable presumption that equitable tolling applies in suits against the United States did not displace these cases: it involved a different statute without a settled construction, did not overrule Soriano, and a definitive earlier construction can rebut the presumption. Franconia concerned accrual, not waiver or tolling. The Court declined to overrule the older cases, since statutory stare decisis has special force where Congress can amend the result and has long acquiesced.

Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Ginsburg, dissented, reasoning that Irwin had already rejected the older framework. Justice Ginsburg also dissented separately and would have overruled the older cases expressly if necessary. The casebook cites the case in distinguishing jurisdictional conditions from merits requirements, and the brief notes that the majority relied on precedent and stare decisis rather than treating the words has jurisdiction as newly decisive.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-132:
The Court drew on Ankenbrandt, which preserved the longstanding domestic-relations exception while limiting it to divorce, alimony and custody decrees. Federal jurisdiction here rested on the bankruptcy grant in § 1334; the Court did not decide whether an uncodified probate exception applies to that grant at all, because Vickie's claim fell outside the exception even assuming it applied.

The central precedent, Markham v. Allen, allowed a federal judgment establishing rights in an estate while protecting the state court's custody of estate property. Some lower courts had expanded its phrase about interfering with the probate proceedings into a broad bar on probate-related matters. The Court read the phrase with the narrower property-custody language beside it: essentially the ordinary rule that two courts may not simultaneously control the same property. Vickie's tort alleged fraudulent interference with a gift, conduct ordinary trial courts can evaluate; she sought neither to annul the will nor to reach property held by the probate court.

Texas law governed the elements of the tort, but Texas could not reserve that transitory claim exclusively to its probate courts and thereby diminish federal jurisdiction, since a court's jurisdiction comes from the law creating that court. The Ninth Circuit's reliance on Durfee v. Duke was misplaced: the contested issue was the federal courts' jurisdiction, not the state court's own.

Justice Stevens concurred in part and in the judgment and would abandon the probate exception altogether. The casebook cites the case in its note on judicially created exceptions to diversity jurisdiction; the brief notes that the casebook's account wrongly gives 1994 as the year of J. Howard's death.

On the first count, jurisdiction turned on the pleaded allegations of interstate employment and the carrier's business in the district; the railroad's denial that Moore worked in interstate commerce went to the merits. Relying on the Safety Appliance Acts did not require abandoning FELA, which itself bars contributory-negligence and assumption-of-risk defenses when a carrier's violation of an employee-safety statute contributes to the injury. Violation of a prescribed safety duty supplied negligence per se within a FELA action.

On the second count, Kentucky's statute largely reproduced FELA's framework for local employment and thereby incorporated the federal equipment requirements into the state cause of action. The court of appeals thought those requirements covered only interstate activity, but the 1903 amendment extended them to vehicles used on any railroad engaged in interstate commerce, so the duty could protect a worker engaged in intrastate activity. That did not make the state action arise under federal law. The Safety Appliance Acts prescribe absolute duties but create no comprehensive remedial system for employee suits; recovery for breach operates through common-law principles or the relevant state statute. FELA drew interstate-employment injuries into its own system, while intrastate injuries remained governed by state liability law.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-146:
Section 1331 does not reach every dispute Article III would permit, and jurisdiction normally follows the plaintiff's well-pleaded complaint. Holmes's proposition that a suit arises under the law creating the cause of action covers the great majority of cases but is not exclusive: a state-created claim can sometimes turn on a sufficiently substantial federal issue. The question was whether this incorporated federal standard supplied one.

The modern implied-remedy inquiry attends to legislative intent, the protected class, statutory purposes and the traditionally state character of the remedy. Allowing a state claim's incorporation of the same federal standard to create federal jurisdiction would, in the majority's view, undermine Congress's assumed decision to withhold a private federal remedy. The Court rejected an automatic test under which any necessary federal ingredient suffices; substantiality and congressional intent must still be examined.

Footnote 12 distinguished Smith, where the state claim challenged the constitutionality of an important federal statute, from Moore v. Chesapeake & Ohio Railway Co., where incorporating a federal safety standard did not fundamentally transform the state tort claim. An interest in uniform interpretation did not justify original jurisdiction, since the Court can review state judgments; preemption is a separate question; and the novelty of applying the FDCA to sales in Canada and Scotland did not create jurisdiction.

Justice Brennan, joined by Justices White, Marshall and Blackmun, dissented. He read Smith to confer jurisdiction whenever resolving a colorable federal question is necessary to recovery, and saw no reason why withholding a federal remedy implied hostility to a federal forum for a state remedy. The casebook excerpts majority footnote 12 and dissent footnote 1; its later discussion of circuit disagreement is editorial.
