An interest in uniform interpretation did not justify original jurisdiction, since the Court can review state judgments; preemption is a separate question; and the novelty of applying the FDCA to sales in Canada and Scotland did not create jurisdiction.

Justice Brennan, joined by Justices White, Marshall and Blackmun, dissented. He read Smith to confer jurisdiction whenever resolving a colorable federal question is necessary to recovery, and saw no reason why withholding a federal remedy implied hostility to a federal forum for a state remedy.
CP-COMP-CB-CAP-149:
Empire had not established a federal common-law basis for this claim. Clearfield involved the Government's own rights and an independently available jurisdictional basis, and later decisions show that federal contracts do not invariably require a uniform federal rule; Boyle requires an identifiable, significant conflict between a federal interest and state law, and Empire identified none governing reimbursement from this settlement. The reimbursement right depended on the enrollee's recovery from third parties, which state tort law determined. FEHBA did not create an express statutory reimbursement right for carriers or expressly give them federal jurisdiction over collection suits; its express jurisdictional provision, § 8912, concerns actions against the United States founded on the Act.

Section 8902(m)(1) makes contract terms on coverage or benefits preempt state law relating to health insurance or plans. It could be read narrowly or as reaching reimbursement, but even the broader reading did not make it a sweeping grant of federal jurisdiction over the carrier's suit, and its unusual reliance on contract terms to preempt state law warranted a modest reading.

Grable concerned a federal agency's action and a comparatively pure legal question that could control other cases. Empire's claim arose from a particular state tort settlement and was fact-bound, and state courts could consider any federal questions that actually arose.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-173:
The Court began by accepting the removal error rather than excusing it. Earlier cases favored preserving some judgments despite improper removal but did not control: in American Fire & Casualty Co. v. Finn jurisdiction remained deficient at judgment, and in Grubbs v. General Electric Credit Corp. no party had objected before trial. Lewis had promptly sought remand and then appealed.

Dismissal of Whayne Supply cured the jurisdictional deficiency, but it did not erase Caterpillar's statutory failure to remove a case fit for federal adjudication at the time of removal. Nor had Lewis waived his objection. His timely remand motion preserved it; he was not required to seek a discretionary §1292(b) interlocutory appeal, a requirement that would be inconsistent with the final-judgment system. His complaint was concrete, since proper adherence to the removal rules would have kept the case in state court.

The controlling consideration was the cost of undoing a completed diversity trial that applied state substantive law and ended with all federal jurisdictional requirements met. Finality, efficiency, and economy weighed strongly against sending the case back, and Newman-Green supported the result. The boundary was essential: had a jurisdictional defect remained at the end, the judgment would have to be vacated.

Lewis warned that the rule would invite premature removal. The Court expected district courts to enforce the removal requirements and thought defendants unlikely to gain from gambling that a defect would escape detection and disappear before judgment.

The casebook presents the case before a contrasting account of Grupo Dataflux; the brief notes that this contrast is the casebook's editorial comparison.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-175:
The bondholders' theory was that an unconstitutional statute is as though it never existed, so there was no jurisdiction and no binding decree. The Court rejected that as too absolute. A statute's actual existence before it is invalidated is an operative fact with consequences for conduct, status, settled rights, and final adjudications, and a later declaration cannot necessarily erase the past.

Apart from Ashton, the elements of the District's preclusion defense were present. The earlier proceeding complied with the statute, its regularity was unchallenged, and the bondholders were parties with notice who could have contested the plan's fairness, the decree's terms, or the statute's validity. Their failure to raise an available objection did not preserve it for a separate action.

The bondholders stressed that the federal court sat in bankruptcy with only statutory jurisdiction. The Court agreed that lower federal courts have limited jurisdiction but denied that every jurisdictional error makes their judgments nullities. A court that has the parties before it consistently with due process has authority to determine whether it may entertain the case, including to construe the statute under which it acts, and that determination is open to direct review, not collateral attack. This applies whether the claim is that the court exceeded a valid statute or that the enabling statute was unconstitutional. Had the bondholders litigated validity and lost, the ruling would have been final; silence could not put them in a better position. Res judicata extends to matters that could have been presented, not only those actually argued.

The casebook cites the case in a note on collateral attack and says the notified parties chose not to appear; the brief notes that the opinion itself establishes party status, notice, and opportunity but does not narrate an appearance history.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-177:
The appellees argued that the Wisconsin court's view that the order was merely erroneous, with no appeal taken, was an adequate nonfederal ground. The Court disagreed: whether the state court's actions were erroneous or beyond its power depended on the meaning of the federal statute, a federal question, and if Congress ousted jurisdiction the lack of a direct appeal could not validate the prohibited actions.

The Court acknowledged the normal presumption of regularity and protection against collateral attack for judgments of competent courts, citing Chicot among other decisions. But Congress's bankruptcy power allowed it to create a specific exception making judicial actions concerning protected debtors or property nullities, and state control of local procedure could not authorize disregard of federal bankruptcy law.

Section 75 did so. Subsection (n) placed the farmer and his property, including unexpired redemption rights and unconfirmed sales, under the bankruptcy court's exclusive jurisdiction. Subsection (o) prohibited commencing or maintaining foreclosure and possession proceedings unless the bankruptcy judge consented after a prescribed process. Subsection (p) applied those prohibitions to judicial and official proceedings. The 1935 amendments and committee reports reinforced this. The scheme aimed to rehabilitate distressed farmers, who did not have to hire counsel; requiring them to seek separate stays would undermine an automatic safeguard. Because the statute itself withdrew power, the confirmation, deed, writ, and ejection lacked authority, and whether the farmer had contested or could have contested jurisdiction was immaterial.

The casebook contrasts the case with Chicot; the brief adds that Kalb is a statutory exception to ordinary finality, not a rule permitting collateral attack whenever jurisdiction is disputed.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-178: In 1956 the Durfees sued in a Nebraska trial court, which quieted title in them after a hearing. On Duke's appeal the Nebraska Supreme Court tried the matter de novo on the existing record and found that Nebraska had jurisdiction and that the Durfees owned the land; Duke did not seek review in the Court. Two months later Duke sued in Missouri, and the case was removed to federal district court on diversity. The district court held the Nebraska judgment res judicata. The Eighth Circuit reversed, allowing renewed examination of Nebraska's jurisdiction. The Court reversed the court of appeals and affirmed the district court. The brief notes that the casebook account attributes the allowance of collateral attack to the district court, whereas the opinion shows that the court of appeals allowed it.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-193:
CPLR 327 authorizes a court, on motion, to stay or dismiss an action on just conditions when substantial justice calls for its resolution elsewhere. The defendant bears the burden. The considerations include the burden on New York courts, hardship to the defendant, the availability of another forum, the parties' nonresidence, and where the underlying transaction occurred, and no single factor controls.

Here Iranian law would probably govern important questions, a New York court's ability to impose an effective constructive trust on foreign property was uncertain, and much of the evidence was in Iran beyond New York's compulsory process. Iran relied on decisions describing an alternative forum as indispensable. The majority treated the relevant language in Gulf Oil as dictum and read New York precedent as making availability one pertinent factor; an absolute requirement would force New York to hear foreign actions unrelated to the State whenever another forum could not or would not. The court did not find that every other forum was unavailable. It said Iran had not established that, and that dismissal was permissible even assuming it. Iran was a sovereign with control over its own legal system and the evidence, not a private claimant shut out of court. An unconditional dismissal was justified.

On the Accords, the United States' undertakings regarding the Shah's assets and enforcement of judgments were not a promise that a New York court would adjudicate the claim, and language about facilitating recovery did not displace ordinary forum rules.

Judge Meyer, dissenting, regarded an available alternative forum as a threshold condition that the defendant must establish, and suggested a conditional stay.

The casebook cites the case in a note; the brief says its account states the absence of an alternative forum more definitively than the opinion does, and that this state-law holding is not the federal adequate-alternative-forum inquiry.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-194:
Because the claims arose from conduct outside Washington, the panel examined general jurisdiction, for which Tuazon needed a prima facie showing. Washington's statute treated continuous and substantial participation in its markets as doing business. Under the circuit's then-applied due-process framework the panel weighed the longevity, continuity, volume, economic impact, physical presence, and local integration of Reynolds's activities, and distinguished sporadic or isolated sales. Reynolds then had the burden of a compelling case of unreasonableness and identified no specific hardship in defending where it had operated for decades. The brief notes that this describes the court's 2006 analysis and does not certify that its general-jurisdiction formulation governs today.

Forum non conveniens requires an adequate alternative and a balance of interests strongly favoring dismissal, with the burden on the defendant. The panel read the record as showing Reynolds's alternative consent to service in the Philippines. The affidavit established potential redress; smaller damages did not make the remedy nonexistent. Tuazon identified no civil proceeding he had personally observed to support his claims of corruption and delay, and the State Department reports principally concerned human rights and criminal justice. The court did not hold that corruption or delay could never defeat adequacy.

Adequacy did not require dismissal. Tuazon's lawful Washington residence entitled his choice to the deference owed a resident plaintiff, and review of the balancing was for clear abuse of discretion. Both parties resided in the United States; evidence of the alleged conspiracy would largely be American and current medical evidence was in Washington; bringing selected Philippine witnesses to Washington would cost less than moving the case abroad. Washington had a local interest in its resident, and the possible application of Philippine law was one factor, not a command to dismiss.

The casebook cites the case in a note; the brief says its suggestion that the Country Report was the plaintiff's only evidence compresses the record.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-196:
The court recited the forum non conveniens sequence: identify an adequate forum with jurisdiction over the whole case, weigh private interests with a presumption for the plaintiff's choice, assess public interests, and ensure the plaintiff can reinstate the suit in the alternative forum without undue prejudice. Adequacy was dispositive. A less generous remedy does not defeat adequacy, but a remedy so unsatisfactory that it amounts to none does.

The Commission could award relief only to Ethiopia or Eritrea, and Eritrea would control any award made on Nemariam's behalf. Under international law a state may abandon, settle, retain, or barter its claim, and the agreement expressly permitted direct negotiations between the governments. Eritrea could therefore offset the claim or an award against Ethiopian claims even if Nemariam's grievance were entirely meritorious. The court agreed that the record did not suggest a planned setoff, but that was not the controlling question: the governments had the option, no legal barrier prevented it, and Ethiopia had not negated the possibility.

Ethiopia pointed to Eritrea's announced intention to pass compensation for private property directly to victims. The court distinguished a voluntary governmental intention from an enforceable right; the Commission could not compel Eritrea to honor that intention. Ethiopia also cited Gonzalez, where limited Mexican wrongful-death recovery made litigation economically unattractive; a modest legal entitlement differs from possibly receiving nothing despite success. By contrast, assuming the district court had jurisdiction, success there would produce relief enforceable by the plaintiff herself.

The casebook cites the case in a note; the brief says the casebook's quotation omits that jurisdictional qualification.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-197:
A defendant seeking foreign-forum dismissal must ordinarily show that the alternative can address the dispute and that the defendant is amenable to process there. A less favorable remedy does not defeat adequacy; it must be so inadequate that it amounts to none. The defendant must also show that convenience and judicial efficiency strongly favor the alternative. Discretionary judgments are reviewed deferentially and legal errors de novo.

The plaintiffs argued that GE's willingness to accept service in Japan was empty because the channeling statute barred recovery against it. The court accepted that consent to service did not by itself resolve the channeling issue, but found that Japan's system addressed the same injuries. Japanese courts remained open to the damage claims against TEPCO, many putative class members had already recovered, and the plaintiffs gave no basis to find compensation effectively nonexistent. Gulf Oil's reference to two forums in which the defendant is amenable to process did not bar every scheme that redirects liability to another party; its concern was a meaningful absence of jurisdiction and relief. Full and fair compensation for the same injury can suffice whoever pays, which the panel analogized to complete recovery from one of two jointly liable tortfeasors. The court also observed, as a supporting inference only, that Massachusetts choice-of-law rules would likely select Japanese law.

The panel upheld reliance on direct claims and mediation, finding instructive the precedents that accept no-fault or administrative systems. The plaintiffs did not challenge the specific adequacy findings about those mechanisms.

The brief stresses that this is not a categorical ruling that any administrative fund is adequate or that a defendant's consent always cures a foreign forum's deficiencies. The casebook cites the case in a note.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-198:
On jurisdiction, an in-state representative's activities can be attributed to a foreign corporation when they are important enough that the corporation would perform them itself without the representative. The office worked entirely for the parents, was funded by them, and cultivated access to capital markets. Listing securities and the tasks ancillary to it do not alone establish general jurisdiction, but this permanent, staffed operation went beyond that. There was no compelling unfairness given the defendants' resources and American presence. The brief notes that this recounts the 2000 holding without certifying the present validity of its general-jurisdiction formula.

On forum non conveniens, the defendant must establish an adequate alternative forum and show that private and public interests strongly favor it. The plaintiffs disputed English adequacy on the basis of several English doctrines; the panel assumed England could reach the merits because the balancing independently required reversal. The district court counted the plaintiffs' lack of residence in the Southern District against them without crediting two plaintiffs' United States residence, which was legal error. Deference grows with a plaintiff's ties because litigating abroad is more likely to cause hardship, and a resident's home forum for this purpose need not be the district of residence. Residence is a practical consideration, not an absolute shield.

The panel also found an American policy favoring a forum for torture claims in the Alien Tort Claims Act as supplemented by the Torture Victim Protection Act, which reinforced the need for strong reasons to dismiss, though the other factors sufficed without it. Starting again in England would impose substantial expense on plaintiffs with minimal resources and pro bono American counsel, while the defendants showed only document-shipping costs and somewhat longer flights for Nigerian witnesses.

The casebook cites the case in a note; the brief says its account compresses the plaintiffs into three emigres living in the United States.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-199:
A defendant seeking forum non conveniens dismissal bears the burden on an adequate and available alternative forum, the balance of private and public interests, and the plaintiff's ability to reinstate the action abroad without undue inconvenience. An American plaintiff's domestic choice receives a strong presumption of convenience that requires substantial evidence of oppression or material injustice to overcome. Foreign plaintiffs receive less deference, but not none.

The court rejected a categorical rule reducing deference because an American invested in a foreign enterprise; that fact does not show where the alleged wrongs occurred or where evidence can be obtained. The unrebutted complaint alleged American direction, communications, personnel, and evidence, and Citigroup's insistence that Mexican entities were responsible substituted its merits theory for the allegations. The presence of thirty-seven foreign coplaintiffs did not dilute the two Americans' presumption: the ratio showed no added burden, and there was no evidence that the Americans were nominal or added through forum gamesmanship. The district court could consider on remand whether separate analysis or severance was warranted.

The second error was evidentiary. Even Piper Aircraft required enough information to evaluate the relevant interests. Citigroup supplied no evidentiary basis establishing the location and materiality of documents or witnesses; general assertions that former Banamex employees or Mexican records were critical did not identify roles, expected testimony, or obstacles. Its materials on Mexico's adequacy, banking secrecy, and corporate organization did not fill that gap. The public-interest analysis also had to account for the Miami activities and the United States' interest in alleged domestic wrongdoing by its corporation against Americans.

The casebook quotes the case in a note on the coplaintiff issue; the brief adds that the opinion's evidence requirement was also decisive.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-200:
Steel Co. generally requires jurisdiction before a merits determination. Ruhrgas, however, rejects an inflexible sequence among threshold grounds for declining to hear a case, allowing personal jurisdiction sometimes to be decided before subject-matter jurisdiction. The Court applied the same distinction to forum non conveniens: the court decides that another forum should hear the merits and does not declare whether the claim succeeds.

A forum non conveniens analysis may require looking at claims, evidence, or defenses, but that overlap does not make it a merits adjudication. Van Cauwenberghe's remark about such overlap concerned the collateral-order doctrine, a different question. The Third Circuit relied on Gulf Oil's statements that the doctrine presupposes jurisdiction and two available forums; read in context, Gulf Oil asked whether an otherwise competent court could decline to adjudicate, not whether jurisdiction must always be resolved first. If a court actually determines that it lacks jurisdiction, it must dismiss on that ground.

The doctrine ordinarily places a heavy burden on the defendant, though the presumption for the plaintiff's choice has less force when the plaintiff sues outside its home forum. Here the subject-matter question was one of first impression, personal-jurisdiction discovery would bring expense and delay, the dispute was already being litigated in China, and its core concerned representations to the Chinese admiralty court. CP-COMP-CB-CAP-215:
The Court applied the Hanna inquiry rather than beginning by mechanically labeling the Alabama penalty substantive or procedural. The first question is whether the federal rule, fairly construed, is broad enough to collide directly with state law or to control the issue, leaving no room for the state rule. If so, the federal rule governs so long as it is a valid exercise of constitutional rulemaking authority and complies with the Rules Enabling Act. This approach applies to federal appellate rules as well as civil rules.

Rule 38's discretionary operation unmistakably conflicted with the statute's mandatory operation. Both addressed compensation and deterrence arising from unsuccessful appeals, so the federal rule occupied the field. A federal court might think some damages justified but less than ten percent; the automatic minimum would defeat that discretion, and allowing a further discretionary award on top of the penalty would not restore it. That Alabama's own rule and statute coexisted did not define a federal court's discretion. The Court found persuasive a Fifth Circuit decision rejecting a similar Mississippi surcharge, and noted in a footnote that federal postjudgment-interest and stay provisions already addressed related concerns.

Rule 38 was valid. It regulated matters reasonably classified as procedural, and its choice of case-by-case enforcement affected the process of enforcing rights rather than the rights themselves. Federal rules carry presumptive validity, and incidental effects on substantive interests do not necessarily violate the Enabling Act.

Flintkote proposed generally applicable insurance-contract principles and said the relevant decisions agreed on full-value coverage. The court rejected that under Erie. The decisions Flintkote invoked applied Illinois or Maryland law, and their disagreement with California did not create a uniform rule. Under Klaxon a diversity court ordinarily applies the forum state's conflicts principles. The court rejected the argument that Delaware's conflicts rules followed the transferred case. In a footnote it treated Flintkote's anticipatory filing to avoid California law as outside the transfer principle Flintkote relied on, analogizing Atlantic Marine's refusal to reward inappropriate forum selection. The brief cautions that this should not be expanded into a claim that every transfer eliminates the transferor's conflicts rules.

Applying California's governmental-interest approach, the court found California had the compelling connection: headquarters, principal location of the risk, and many asbestos suits. Delaware's incorporation and trust-administration interests did not turn interpretation of much older policies into a question of the Trust's internal operation. The court also cited Flintkote's own earlier arguments for California law and the final parallel arbitration ruling favoring California.

Fuller-Austin then controlled. The policies indemnified sums Flintkote was obligated to pay by law, and the Trust was obligated to pay only the percentage. Public policy favoring asbestos compensation could not enlarge the coverage, and a waiver of exclusionary defenses did not enlarge the insuring agreement's initial scope.

On the bond, Aviva's section 1620(a) exception failed for want of affirmative evidence of compliance with the asserted foreign jurisdictions' laws.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-241:
The railroad argued that state courts must preserve federal substantive rights but stay free to use their own practice and procedure. Justice Black did not attempt a comprehensive line between substance and procedure. The Court's precedents required independent scrutiny of the complaint to see whether state practice had denied a federally granted opportunity for trial; a federal right could not be eliminated by the form of local pleading rules.

Read fairly, the complaint alleged a known dangerous accumulation, a duty to provide a reasonably safe workplace, a direction to work there, and an injury suffered while crossing it. Those allegations could support evidence from which a jury might infer negligence; an earlier case had upheld a Georgia judgment resting on such an inference from clinkers beside tracks. Georgia's court had drawn the opposite inference at the pleading stage, and its focus on Brown's failure to see the clinker was especially problematic because contributory negligence does not bar recovery under the Act. Over-exacting local pleading requirements could burden federal rights and undermine their uniform adjudication.

Justice Frankfurter agreed a state could not shut its courts to federal claims or impair federal rights through procedural disguises, but thought states could keep pleading formalities applied equally to comparable local claims, just as federal courts enforcing state rights use federal procedures. He believed Georgia understood the Act's standards and saw only a failure to plead with the particularity Georgia demanded. Because Brown could have amended and chose not to, he would have affirmed.

The casebook cites the case in a note after Dice, quoting its protection of federal rights and asking about the opportunity to replead; the brief adds that Brown does not hold that every state proceeding under a federal statute must use federal procedure.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-245:
Lord Kenyon treated the relation between the defendant's act and the injury as controlling. An injury produced by the immediate act complained of belonged in trespass; an injury merely consequential on that act belonged in case. The classification did not turn on counsel's description of the underlying activity as lawful or of its performance as negligent.

He illustrated the rule with a log thrown into the highway. If the log struck the plaintiff as it was thrown, the injury was immediate and trespass would lie. If the log later lay in the road and the plaintiff stumbled over it, case was the remedy for the consequential injury. The example separates an injury inflicted by the operative act from a later injury caused by the condition the act created.

Applying that distinction, the declaration alleged that Edwards personally drove the cart so that it struck and overturned Day's carriage. Calling the driving negligent, or inserting the phrase "in consequence," did not turn that direct impact into consequential harm of the log-in-the-road kind.

The casebook places Day among the cases in which the immediate-versus-consequential distinction met negligence and accidents; the brief states the lesson as being that negligence alone did not make case the proper form under Kenyon's rule in 1794, and that later flexibility belongs to other decisions.

The court's reasoning focused on the identity of the defendant. It was difficult to regard a master as a trespasser for an act of his servant that had not been done at the master's command. Although the cart directly hit the chaise, that immediate contact did not settle whether the master himself was answerable in trespass. The court nevertheless granted a rule to show cause out of respect for the King's Bench decisions that counsel had cited, so it could consider the point further. When the matter returned a few days later, counsel conceded that the rule could not be supported, and the court agreed, expressing the clear view that case was the proper form.

The brief cautions that Morley should not be expanded into a rule that all negligent direct injuries must be pleaded in case: the controversy involved a defendant whose servant drove the cart, and the court's stated concern was whether a master could be treated as the direct trespasser without a command. Later editorial annotations printed with the report, which propose distinctions drawn from subsequent cases, are not the court's words.

The casebook cites the case for the master-servant distinction and contrasts it with later collision decisions debating immediate injury and negligent conduct.

Lord Kenyon kept the immediate-versus-consequential distinction and expressly accepted that a defendant's mind need not concur in the act for trespass to lie. But he did not regard the record as showing that the defendants themselves committed the immediately injurious act. The charge was that negligent steering and management caused the collision, and on that account liability could be pursued in case. He distinguished the personal acts alleged in Day and Savignac; he did not adopt a rule that every unintentional collision belongs in case.

Justice Grose stressed timing. On a motion in arrest of judgment, presumptions favor the verdict. The declaration charged negligence, not willful action. He compared Morley, where case was accepted, with Tripe v. Potter, where willful action made case inappropriate. Had the evidence shown willful conduct, the plaintiffs should have been nonsuited at trial; since the jury found for them, the court should take the pleaded negligence as proved.

Justice Lawrence likewise treated willfulness and negligence differently on this record. Negligent management did not necessarily mean the defendants did the immediate act: after earlier negligence they might have done everything possible to avoid harm, with wind and tide driving their ship into the other. That was an illustration of what the record allowed, not a finding.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-253:
Lord Mansfield said he disapproved of nonsuits founded on objections unrelated to a cause's merits, but considered that principles and authorities controlled here: the proper action was case rather than trover. He likened the wharfinger's position to that of a common carrier, because both receive goods upon a contract. What trover required was an injurious conversion, not simply a failure to perform the obligation to return the goods. The defendants could not deliver these lost or stolen goods; delivery was no longer within their power. Their omission therefore differed from withholding goods they were able to return.

Justice Aston agreed that this bare omission supplied no evidence of conversion and that the clear remedy was case. He cited Owen v. Lewyn for Hale's statement that general trover would not lie against a carrier who lost goods committed to him. Justices Willes and Ashhurst concurred.

The brief notes the limits of the reasoning. It is not a finding that the defendants intentionally appropriated the goods, a general immunity for negligent bailees, or a judgment for damages in case. Nor did the court require conversion always to be shown by direct evidence; it concluded that an inability to return lost goods did not establish the necessary conversion here.

The casebook's note reproduces the central distinction between injurious conversion and bare omission, applied to goods entrusted to wharfingers and then lost or stolen.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-345:
The majority treated the injury as unequal competition. A person challenging a discriminatory barrier need not prove that removing it would guarantee success; the injury is the inability to compete on equal terms. Answering Justice Stevens, the majority distinguished a new practice presenting materially different concerns from a shared policy applied through different entry routes. The transfer guidelines cross-referenced the diversity criteria used in freshman admissions, and both treated membership in an underrepresented racial group as a contribution to diversity. Differences in mechanics could matter to narrow tailoring but did not defeat standing to challenge the common diversity justification. The Court contrasted General Telephone Co. of Southwest v. Falcon, where an individual promotion claim and class hiring claims rested on different proof. The majority acknowledged a possible tension between Article III standing and Rule 23(a) adequacy but did not resolve which doctrine governed, finding the requirements satisfied here.

On the merits, the Court rejected, for the reasons given in Grutter, the argument that diversity could never justify racial preferences, but the 20-point bonus did not assess each applicant's individual contribution and made race decisive for virtually every minimally qualified underrepresented applicant. The review committee was an exception operating after points were assigned, and administrative difficulty did not relax strict scrutiny.

Justice O'Connor concurred, contrasting the law school's individualized evaluation; Justice Thomas concurred; Justice Breyer concurred only in the judgment. Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Souter, would have dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because neither plaintiff had the necessary prospective stake. Justice Souter argued that Hamacher had no stake in the narrow-tailoring challenge and that the system resembled a permissible plus-factor program. Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justice Souter, would have affirmed on the merits. CP-COMP-CB-CAP-352:
Section 1291's final-judgment rule avoids repeated interruptions, expense and delay, and a certification decision is ordinarily interlocutory. Coopers & Lybrand v. Livesay rejected the death-knell approach that treated class denial as final when individual litigation was impractical. Rule 23(f), adopted in 1998 after Congress authorized rulemaking on interlocutory appeals, deliberately made review of class orders discretionary with the court of appeals. Finality must be construed in light of that structure, not solely by whether a document purports to close a case.

The majority identified three defects. First, the device invited repeated interlocutory appeals at the plaintiffs' sole election: if they won and certification was again denied on another ground, they could repeat the procedure, as the Ninth Circuit's comity-only ruling illustrated. The plaintiffs' willingness to risk their claims did not protect the system, since weak claims and the settlement value of certification could make the risk attractive; the majority did not find these claims weak. Second, mandatory review through dismissal would defeat Rule 23(f), letting plaintiffs bypass a denial of discretionary review they had requested. Third, the tactic was one-sided, because defendants could not similarly force review of an adverse certification grant.

Justice Thomas, concurring in the judgment, thought the dismissal with prejudice satisfied § 1291 but found no Article III controversy: by dismissing, the plaintiffs consented to judgment and disclaimed relief, and class allegations are a procedural mechanism, not an independent claim. The brief notes that one casebook account compresses the Ninth Circuit's comity ruling into a reversal of the certification denial, and that the other wrongly says the district court, not the Ninth Circuit, denied Rule 23(f) permission.

The FAA makes covered agreements enforceable subject to grounds for revoking a contract, and the Court emphasized enforcing agreed terms, including with whom the parties arbitrate and under what procedures. The Sherman and Clayton Acts did not guarantee affordable pursuit of every claim or prohibit waiving class procedure; they predated Rule 23, and congressional approval of that rule created no entitlement to a class proceeding whenever one was financially necessary.

The merchants invoked the judge-made principle against arbitration terms that prospectively waive federal statutory remedies. The Court described the relevant Mitsubishi discussion as dictum but explained the distinction. A clause forbidding assertion of specified statutory rights would fall within the concern, and filing or administrative fees so high as to make access impracticable might also qualify. Making proof uneconomic is different from eliminating the right to pursue the remedy, and the class waiver only limited the proceeding to the contracting parties. The Court did not decide whether a prohibition on economic testimony would be an invalid waiver. Concepcion strongly supported the result, and requiring pre-arbitration litigation of proof costs and expected recovery would undermine the streamlined resolution arbitration is meant to supply.

Justice Thomas, concurring, read the FAA's revocation exception as addressing defects in making the agreement, such as fraud or duress, which the merchants did not assert. Justice Kagan, dissenting, argued that effective vindication prevents indirect as well as express prospective waivers. She viewed the contract as a whole, including bars on joinder and consolidation, confidentiality and no cost shifting, as foreclosing every way of sharing, shifting or shrinking costs, and distinguished Concepcion as a state-preemption case. The majority disputed that broader account of the contract. The brief notes that one casebook account wrongly describes the case as a California unconscionability ruling; the casebook otherwise correctly identifies the issue as proof costs exceeding potential recovery.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-367:
The court applied Rule 26(b)(1): discovery must be relevant to a claim or defense and proportional, considering the importance of the issues, amount in controversy, relative access, resources, importance of the discovery and burden against benefit. Information within that scope need not be admissible. The movant first had to establish relevance; the opposing party then had to justify why the particular request was improper.

Discovery of O'Gara's own file was obviously relevant, and Equifax had omitted requested details. Five years of mixed-file counts, lawsuits and disputes were relevant to whether Equifax knew of recurring problems and still failed to use reasonable procedures; similar complaints could lead to evidence of negligence or willfulness even if not themselves admissible. Proportionality was assessed separately. Verdicts in other FCRA cases did not establish the amount at stake, and Equifax mostly recited the factors without specific evidence of burden, which was insufficient. By contrast, requests for every accuracy study without time limits were denied, as were requests about procedures already answered through produced manuals where O'Gara identified no shortcomings.

The New York investigation was relevantly connected to the alleged public-record matching problem, and the low overall incidence of mixed files did not make it irrelevant, but discovery was narrowed to mixed files with O'Gara's particular public-record problem. Equifax's subsequent-remedial-measure objection was waived for discoverability because it was not timely raised, and in any event admissibility under Evidence Rule 407 was a separate question from discoverability. Given the mixed outcome, the court exercised its discretion under Rule 37(a)(5) to have each side bear its own costs. The casebook uses the case for the relevance of similar mixed-file disputes; the brief notes that the Westlaw citation the casebook prints does not appear in the actual docket order.

Rule 34 covered electronic data, including recoverable deleted material. UBS could not establish completeness by pointing to its search of employees' current files, and Zubulake's possession of some messages did not show she had the rest.

The court distinguished five storage categories: active online data, near-line data, offline storage or archives, backup tapes, and erased or fragmented data. The first three generally were accessible; the last two generally required restoration or processing. Electronic discovery could be cheaper and easier than paper discovery, and automatically shifting costs threatened to price plaintiffs out of meritorious cases.

Revising Rowe's eight-factor approach, the court set out seven factors: how specifically the request targets relevant information; whether other sources can supply it; production cost compared with the amount in controversy; production cost compared with each party's resources; each party's ability and incentive to control cost; the importance of the issues in the litigation; and the relative benefit to each party. They are not weighed equally. The first two form the central marginal-utility inquiry, the next three address expense and who can bear it, the sixth arises infrequently but could predominate, and the seventh is least important. The court rejected absolute cost and relative wealth as sufficient measures and generally discarded the purpose for which data was retained. The guiding question was whether the request imposed undue burden or expense relative to the information's importance.

Sampling supplied actual evidence of responsive material and restoration expense, and the court rejected requiring advance proof that discovery would yield a gold mine. The casebook reproduces the seven factors and the $175,000 estimate; the brief notes that it omits the accessible and inaccessible distinction, the unequal weighting and the five-tape sample.

Electronic discovery should ordinarily be driven by the parties. Rule 26(f)(3)(C) expressly requires counsel to confer about disclosure, discovery and preservation of electronically stored information, including the forms of production. The court drew on Romero and its quotation of Trusz concerning practical agreement on terms, dates and relevant people. Local Civil Rule 26.2(C) more specifically required counsel to confer and attempt agreement on protocols, including filters such as terms and date ranges. Cooperation was consistent with these obligations, and the court should not need to manage every search detail. Pyle's argument that no authority supported cooperation therefore failed. The order did not prescribe particular terms, decide the adequacy of a completed search, require predictive coding, or establish that every document matching a keyword must be produced.

On the medical motion, a party's expected compliance is not yet a failure warranting a preemptive production order. CP-COMP-CB-CAP-382:
The court began with the interests protected by Hickman v. Taylor and codified in Rule 26(b)(3): lawyers need room to prepare without surrendering their investigation and analysis. Fact work product ordinarily required substantial need and inability to obtain its equivalent without undue hardship, and opinion work product in the Fourth Circuit approached immunity except in rare and extraordinary circumstances.

But Rule 26(b)(3) was subject to the expert-discovery provisions of Rule 26(b)(4). Read with the 1993 version of Rule 26(a)(2)(B), those provisions required disclosure of information an expert considered in forming an opinion. The Fourth Circuit had not squarely resolved the interaction, so the court treated the 1993 amendments and their Advisory Committee Note as controlling guides. The note explained that material furnished for use in forming an opinion could not be withheld simply because the expert did not ultimately rely on it, and it drew no distinction between fact and opinion work product in that setting.

Policy supported disclosure. An expert's apparent expertise makes effective cross-examination important, particularly where an advocate may have selected the information presented, and the opponent needs to know whether the expert assessed the facts independently or worked from a lawyer's account. Counsel can control the consequence by keeping private legal analysis separate from what is given to the expert. A test confined to actual reliance would require inquiry into the expert's internal thought processes and leave counsel uncertain, so the operative inquiry was consideration.

The small amount of opinion work product in the memoranda reinforced the result; the ordinary substantial-need test was not the governing basis. The casebook reproduces the disclosure rule and cross-examination rationale and then asks, as editorial commentary, whether the rule survives Rule 26(b)(4)(C), adopted in 2010; the brief presents the case as an interpretation of the rules then in force.

The Fourth Circuit had not squarely resolved the interaction, so the court treated the 1993 amendments and their Advisory Committee Note as controlling guides. The note explained that material furnished for use in forming an opinion could not be withheld simply because the expert did not ultimately rely on it, and it drew no distinction between fact and opinion work product in that setting.

Policy supported disclosure. An expert's apparent expertise makes effective cross-examination important, particularly where an advocate may have selected the information presented, and the opponent needs to know whether the expert assessed the facts independently or worked from a lawyer's account. Counsel can control the consequence by keeping private legal analysis separate from what is given to the expert. A test confined to actual reliance would require inquiry into the expert's internal thought processes and leave counsel uncertain, so the operative inquiry was consideration.

The small amount of opinion work product in the memoranda reinforced the result; the ordinary substantial-need test was not the governing basis. The casebook reproduces the disclosure rule and cross-examination rationale and then asks whether the rule survives Rule 26(b)(4)(C), adopted in 2010; the case interprets the rules then in force.
CP-COMP-CB-CAP-385:
Federal courts have inherent authority to sanction bad-faith abuse of the judicial process, and reimbursing the opposing party's legal expenses is one permissible sanction. But when a court uses ordinary civil procedures, the award must compensate and not punish; punishment requires the procedural protections applicable to criminal proceedings. Compensation follows the injury actually caused. If the same work would have been necessary even with proper discovery, shifting its cost adds punishment. The Court drew this framework from Fox v. Vice.

The test does not require perfect accounting. A trial judge may estimate, allocate percentages or treat a category of expenses as caused entirely by the misconduct, and appellate review is deferential, but flexibility in calculation does not dispense with causation. An award of every fee can satisfy the test in an exceptional case, for example where the whole suit was brought in bad faith, where a defendant's entire course of conduct was a scheme to defeat a valid claim, or where the court finds that proper disclosure would have produced settlement at a specific point. These apply the but-for rule; they are not exceptions for extreme behavior.

Here the district court let severity replace causation, and the Ninth Circuit used the period of bad faith as its limit; concurrent timing was not enough. The Court declined to supply a finding that timely disclosure would have ended the suit: the district court had said only that settlement probably would have come much earlier, and Goodyear retained plausible defenses, such as that the tire failed from striking road debris. The district court's own alternative award recognized that roughly $700,000 would have been incurred regardless.

The casebook cites the case for the compensatory limit and the rejected comprehensive award; the brief notes that the casebook's statement that Rule 37 sanctions were unavailable because the suit had settled is editorial explanation.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-458:
Rule 50 supplies two stages. The preverdict motion identifies the claim for judgment as a matter of law and its grounds; if the case goes to the jury, Rule 50(b) gives the postverdict opportunity to renew the legal questions and lets the judge choose among letting the verdict stand, ordering a new trial, or entering judgment as a matter of law.

The Court relied on Cone, Globe Liquor and Johnson, which required a proper postverdict motion before an appellate court could direct judgment against the verdict, and extended their rationale to a sufficiency-based request for a new trial. In either situation the trial judge, with firsthand knowledge of the witnesses, testimony and course of trial, should first assess the requested relief, and renewal serves fairness. The earlier litigants who received new trials had actually sought them after the verdict in the district court.

A Rule 50(a) motion does not ask for a new trial; the new-trial option arises when the court rules on the renewed motion. The district court also had discretion to take the verdict rather than grant judgment immediately, which can reduce retrials, so letting the jury decide was not itself error. ConAgra had every incentive to renew, because judgment in its favor indisputably required renewal. The Court assumed without deciding that the preverdict motion reached every antitrust element.

Justice Stevens, joined by Justice Kennedy, dissented: failure to make proper motions ordinarily entails waiver or forfeiture but does not eliminate appellate power, under 28 U.S.C. section 2106, to correct exceptional injustice. The majority answered that its precedents had already reconciled section 2106 with strict Rule 50 compliance.

The brief notes that the casebook's summary, which says the defendant failed to seek a new trial, omits the damages-only new-trial motion, and that the decision is not a requirement that every civil appeal be preceded by a postverdict motion.

Law of the case barred re-examining liability absent exceptional circumstances, and none were shown.

On newly discovered evidence, the court listed five requirements: probable effect on the result, discovery since trial, inability to discover it before trial through due diligence, materiality, and that it be more than merely cumulative or impeaching. It added a temporal requirement that the evidence concern facts existing at the time of trial. Lewy's technique failed that requirement even though it was developed before the 1965 damages judgment. The earlier mandate also gave the trial court broad discretion in how to determine damages; it could use the existing record, and it had carefully considered the uncertain permanence of the suggested improvement. Denial was therefore not an abuse whether the motions were characterized under Rule 59, 60(b)(2), or 60(b)(6).

On damages, the court refused to make its own findings from evidence it had not heard. Alaska Civil Rule 52(a) required findings detailed enough to explain the award and permit review, and the findings did not explain the differing amounts for impairment and lost earnings well enough. It reserved the parties' opposite claims that the total was inadequate or excessive, but found no clear error in the pain-and-suffering awards. The fee award lacked any explanation for departing from the Rule 82(a) schedule, which did not permit arbitrary departures.

The casebook excerpts the case for the newly discovered evidence rule; the brief notes that the excerpt omits the overall vacatur, the damages remand, and the fee issue.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-464:
The majority acknowledged the historical rule against modifying final judgments after the court term, and that finality ordinarily serves society by ending litigation. But equitable relief against sufficiently serious, later-discovered fraud developed alongside that rule and is flexible, because its purpose is to correct exceptional injustice.

The fraud here met that standard. It was not a mere allegation that a witness might have committed perjury; Hartford's own sworn admissions and the documentary record established a planned scheme to mislead both the Patent Office and the appellate court, and no innocent purchaser had acquired an intervening interest. Hazel's possible lack of maximum diligence did not excuse Hartford, because the integrity of patent proceedings and of the administration of justice implicates public interests beyond the litigants' private stakes. The Court refused to calculate how much the false attribution affected the earlier judges: Hartford had deliberately deployed the article and could not now minimize its effect or excuse the deception by claiming the article's statements were true.

As to power, if the appellate court could finally deny relief long after its judgment, it could also finally grant relief when undisputed fraud on that very court required it. The Court did not authorize final resolution of genuinely disputed material fraud facts on ex parte affidavits without examination and cross-examination; Hartford had not disputed the documents' accuracy.

Justice Roberts, joined by Justices Reed and Frankfurter, dissented. He agreed the fraud was reprehensible but would have reversed with directions to permit Hazel to file a bill in the district court, stressing finality, live testimony, cross-examination, and the diligence and clean-hands requirements. Chief Justice Stone agreed with the result Roberts proposed.

The brief says the casebook's excerpt captures the organized-fraud and public-integrity rationale.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-465:
Where perjured testimony may have played a part in inducing a judgment, the court must confront whether the judgment was obtained partly through perjury. Once that is established, the judge cannot save the judgment by weighing how much the perjury mattered, because the taint reaches the judicial proceeding itself. By refusing to hear further testimony from witnesses who were willing to give it, the district judge avoided the direct inquiry that was required. The appellate court expressly found no indication that any counsel took part in wrongdoing.

The court did not treat every allegation of perjury as sufficient. It distinguished Parker v. Checker Taxi Company, which involved a bare petition verified by attorneys on information and belief with no further proof. Here there were 110 pages of affidavits, witnesses willing to testify after being advised of their constitutional rights, and unimpeached sworn testimony already given in open court. That record so clearly supported the motion that denying it fell outside sound discretion. Rule 60(b) reinforced the court's power to relieve a party from a judgment obtained through fraud, misrepresentation, or an adverse party's misconduct.

The casebook note quotes the court's refusal to weigh the influence of perjury once it helped procure the judgment; the brief cautions that the case should not be reduced to automatic vacatur on an unsupported accusation.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-473:
On service, section 38a-25 supplied substituted service through the commissioner, but its subsection (e) preserved service in any other legally permitted manner; reading the statute to exclude a designated agent would leave that subsection without work. The court acknowledged a textual difficulty, because section 38a-27 also cross-referenced other sections that a broad reading could make redundant. It resolved the difficulty by reading the connected provisions as remedial legislation meant to protect Connecticut insureds from having to pursue unauthorized insurers in distant forums. Liberal construction supported contractual-agent service, and it would be illogical to exclude a contractually authorized method likely to reach the insurers promptly.

On the industrial-insured objection, the defendants relied on section 38a-271(c)(5), but subsection (b)(2) excluded lawful reinsurance transactions from sections 38a-271 through 38a-278. Read together, that exclusion prevented the defendants from applying the industrial-insured exception to these reinsurance contracts.

On the amount, section 38a-27 did not say hearing, but its requirements of court approval and a court-fixed amount were construed to include one, avoiding the constitutional danger of a literal reading. Under Doehr's prejudgment-remedy analysis the court considered the private interest affected, the risk of error and useful safeguards, and the interest of the party seeking the remedy. Prepleading security impairs a defendant's use of property before liability is determined, much as prejudgment attachment does. The closely similar New York statute, upheld with safeguards including an opportunity to be heard, was persuasive support.

The casebook uses the case for the hearing requirement; the brief notes that the casebook omits the two statutory holdings needed to reach it.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-474:
An appellant must show reversible error on an adequate record, silence in the record supports presumptions favoring the order, and a trial court's resolution of factual conflicts in affidavits is not disturbed on appeal.

Attachment generally required a money claim on an express or implied contract for a fixed or readily ascertainable sum of at least $500. Section 484.090 required an eligible claim, probable validity, a proper purpose, and an amount to be secured greater than zero; under section 481.190 probable validity means the claimant is more likely than not to obtain judgment. Section 483.015(b)(2) required the secured amount to be reduced by an indebtedness asserted in a filed cross-complaint if the defendant's claim was itself one upon which an attachment could issue.

That qualifying language decided the case. A claim upon which attachment could issue must satisfy the same probable-validity requirement. Otherwise any defendant could defeat a well-supported attachment by asserting a speculative counterclaim, frustrating the Legislature's provision of prejudgment security.

The trial judge implicitly found Martinez's claims insufficient. The record showed the judge noticed the offsets, heard argument, and said the documentation would be considered, so the appellate court presumed the pertinent evidence was considered. Williams's conclusory assertions about retained funds and 200,000 pounds of steel were contradicted by accounting records and contemporaneous delivery logs. Lydig's own showing was supported by declarations and documentation. The decision does not forbid offsets generally; it requires evidence meeting the statutory standard.

The casebook uses the case as an unsuccessful attempt to defeat attachment through an offset exceeding the applicant's claim; the brief notes that the casebook's term for the standard should be read as probable validity.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-475:
A preliminary injunction is extraordinary relief, not an entitlement that follows automatically from a plausible legal claim, and a mere possibility of harm is too permissive a standard. The Court did not simply find that plaintiffs had proved no environmental danger: it was uncertain whether the Ninth Circuit's incorrect verbal standard affected its analysis, since that court had also affirmed a finding of near-certain harm, and the lower court had not reassessed residual harm after the four unchallenged restrictions. It held that even a showing of irreparable injury would not overcome the balance of equities and public interest on this record, and so did not resolve likely merits success.

The majority credited detailed declarations from senior Navy officers. Courts must give appropriate deference to military judgments about readiness, though military interests do not invariably prevail. The 2,200-yard shutdown radius increased the covered surface area more than one hundredfold over the 200-yard requirement, and one interruption could waste a scenario that took days to develop. Surface ducting was rare, which made training under it harder to replace, and a six-decibel reduction was a seventy-five-percent power reduction. The same balance would preclude a permanent injunction imposing these restrictions; a court could consider declaratory relief or relief tailored to preparation of an environmental impact statement.

Justice Breyer, joined by Justice Stevens in Part I only, also concluded the challenged injunction lacked adequate support, but in Part II would have retained the modified mitigation conditions of the Ninth Circuit's temporary stay until an acceptable statement was complete. Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justice Souter, would have affirmed, emphasizing NEPA's requirement of review before action and defending equitable flexibility and a sliding-scale approach.

The brief notes that the casebook accurately states the four factors and the rejection of a mere possibility of irreparable injury, but that its short account should not be read as a finding that plaintiffs lacked likely injury or that the Navy prevailed on NEPA compliance.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-478:
On mootness, a permanent injunction ordinarily supersedes a preliminary one, but Grupo asserted a potential bond claim for harm from an unauthorized pre-judgment freeze. Winning the contract suit did not show that the earlier asset dispositions were unlawful, so a restraint designed to secure a future judgment could be wrongful even if the eventual judgment was valid.

On the merits, federal equity power under the Judiciary Act derives from the traditional principles and remedies of English Chancery at the founding, and Rule 65 regulates procedure without enlarging the available remedies. The historical creditor's bill generally required a creditor first to obtain a judgment; an unsecured claimant had no cognizable interest in particular debtor property. That requirement protected substantive property rights, and merging law and equity did not eliminate it. The majority distinguished Deckert, which sought equitable rescission and restitution, and First National City Bank, which involved a tax-enforcement statute and a governmental equitable lien, and noted De Beers's warning against unrelated asset freezes. England's Mareva injunctions emerged in 1975 as a substantial departure from earlier practice. Whether to authorize so substantial a new remedy, with its effects on state attachment rules, creditor races and bankruptcy law, was a policy choice for Congress.

Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justices Stevens, Souter and Breyer, agreed on mootness but would have affirmed. She read the grant of equity power as incorporating adaptable principles rather than freezing remedies at eighteenth-century practice, and emphasized safeguards such as a strong merits showing, substantiated danger of noncollection, and a bond.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-485:
Colorado's constitution allowed certain exceptions to the prohibition of imprisonment for debt, but that provision was not self-executing, so legislative authorization was needed, and the statute's age and presumptive validity did not insulate it. Wealth alone was not generally a suspect classification, but the court did not need to choose a stricter standard because the statute failed rational-basis review.

The statute's coercive purpose was to obtain payment. An indigent debtor cannot comply, so confinement punishes without achieving collection, leaves the debt outstanding, and prevents gainful employment. A solvent debtor can buy release; the apparent equal opportunity to pay is illusory for someone who is indigent. Williams and Tate reinforced the discriminatory effect of turning inability to pay into incarceration. But findings of the original tort alone were not a constitutionally sufficient basis for civil detention, since confinement would then punish the wrong without criminal procedural protections. The added probable-cause findings connect detention to preserving recovery. The court acknowledged that it could not authoritatively construe state law and predicted that North Carolina's highest court would adopt this saving construction.

The twenty-day notice rule could keep a debtor obviously without assets confined, letting vengeance rather than disclosure drive detention. Preliminary release differs from final discharge: the creditor can continue investigating, and a later finding of fraudulent concealment could lead to imprisonment until full disclosure.

A state statute supplied counsel to indigent persons in civil arrest proceedings, so the court did not decide whether there was an independent constitutional right to counsel. Miller had acted in good faith, so damages against her were denied.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-493:
Section 1291 ordinarily postpones appeal until a final decision. Cohen permits a small class of orders that conclusively decide important questions separate from the merits and are effectively unreviewable after final judgment, but the exception must not swallow the rule, because piecemeal appeals delay litigation and burden courts. The inquiry is categorical: whether waiting so imperils the interest that immediate appeal should be available for the whole class of orders, not whether one litigant suffers hardship.

The Court acknowledged the privilege's importance but concluded that postjudgment remedies generally suffice: an appellate court can vacate an adverse judgment and order a new trial excluding the improperly disclosed material and its fruits. It doubted that deferring review meaningfully reduces clients' candor, since clients weigh the privilege's scope and exceptions rather than the remote chance of an erroneous order.

Other safeguards remain for serious errors: section 1292(b) certification, mandamus for exceptional usurpation or clear abuse, and refusing disclosure and incurring sanctions or, in appropriate circumstances, contempt. Protective orders can limit spillover. The costs of successive appeals outweighed the limited benefits. The Court declined to decide the government's proposal concerning certain governmental privileges. Any further avenue of appeal should come through the rulemaking process Congress authorized.

Justice Thomas agreed with the outcome but declined the remaining Cohen analysis, considering Congress's choice of rulemaking sufficient reason not to add this category of appeals.

The brief says the casebook's account accurately identifies the adverse privilege disclosure order and the availability of postjudgment review, while omitting the alternative review mechanisms and reservations.

The D.C. Circuit had stressed that disqualification is disruptive, that lawyers may need to vindicate their reputations, and that disqualification motions can be used tactically. The Court acknowledged these concerns but refused to treat them as an independent source of jurisdiction. Interlocutory civil appeals themselves cause delay, as the stay here showed. A lawyer's wish for vindication may diverge from the client's interest. Section 1292(b) certification, exceptional mandamus, and review after final judgment remain available. If mistakes and added expense alone justified immediate appeal, the exception would overwhelm finality.

Applying the reasoning of Flanagan, the criminal-disqualification decision: if erroneous disqualification requires no showing of prejudice for reversal, it can be reviewed as effectively after final judgment as before trial; if prejudice must be shown, the inquiry into its effect on the outcome is inseparable from the merits. On either premise a collateral-order requirement fails. Civil disqualification orders also often overlap the merits, as with lawyer-witness and misconduct issues, and the analysis is categorical.

Justice Brennan concurred on the understanding that appellate courts would develop review standards effectively protecting a litigant's qualified right to chosen counsel. Justice Stevens dissented: he considered the loss of chosen counsel separate from the merits and practically impossible to remedy later, and would have affirmed the D.C. Circuit. Justice Powell did not participate.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-495:
Section 1291 ordinarily permits appeal only after a decision ends the litigation on the merits. Cohen's small collateral category requires conclusiveness, an important issue completely separate from the merits, and effective unreviewability after final judgment, and all three must be met.

On immunity, Van Cauwenberghe relied on the extradition principle of specialty and analogized his claim to qualified immunity, which protects against trial itself. The Court asked whether freedom from the burdens of trial was an essential feature of the claimed protection; otherwise every potentially successful dismissal argument would support immediate appeal. Specialty chiefly governs treaty obligations between states, and a private civil trial does not significantly implicate them before a binding judgment is enforced. Unlike a prosecution, it involves no pretrial detention or bail. He conceded that proper service abroad, or service during unrelated business in the United States, could have required him to defend the same suit. The claim was therefore a right not to be subjected to a binding judgment without valid personal jurisdiction, which later review can vindicate.

On forum non conveniens, weighing access to evidence, witnesses, local interests and applicable law requires examining the underlying allegations and defenses, so the question generally overlaps the merits. CP-COMP-CB-CAP-496:
Denying dismissal kept the litigation going, so the company needed the narrow collateral-order exception: a conclusive decision, an important issue entirely separate from the merits, and effective unreviewability after final judgment. Failure of the third condition disposed of the case.

The company argued the contract gave it both a right to trial in Italy and a right not to be sued elsewhere, and that an appeal after a New York trial could not undo the inconvenience and expense. The Court acknowledged that later correction would not perfectly preserve the bargain, but that is true whenever an interlocutory ruling is mistaken; litigation costs do not overcome Congress's finality requirement. The exception requires a right essentially destroyed by postponing vindication.

The Court contrasted rights not to be tried at all, such as double jeopardy, Speech or Debate protection and civil immunity from suit, with rights to insist on litigation elsewhere. Even on the company's most favorable formulation, a right to be sued only in Naples is not a right to avoid suit altogether, and it is at least as vindicable after judgment as an objection to personal jurisdiction. The federal policy favoring forum-selection clauses invoked under The Bremen goes to enforceability on the merits, not to the timing of review.

Justice Scalia joined the opinion and concurred separately: later reversal does not literally preserve the right to avoid a New York trial, but later vindication is legally adequate because the law does not regard this forum right as important enough to overcome the policies against interlocutory appeals.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-500:
The collateral-order doctrine requires conclusive determination of the disputed question, resolution of an important issue completely separate from the merits, and effective unreviewability after final judgment. Class-certification orders fail for three independent reasons: under the then-applicable Rule 23(c)(1) class status could be revised before the merits decision, so the order was inherently tentative; certification questions such as typicality, adequacy and commonality overlap the merits; and the named plaintiff or intervening class members can obtain effective review after final judgment.

On the death knell, the Court did not deny that decertification might induce abandonment, but refused to make that prediction a substitute for legal finality. The theory would reach discovery, venue or summary-judgment rulings that make litigation economically unattractive, and would make jurisdiction depend on litigants' resources, claim size and costs. An amount-based threshold would be arbitrary and judicially created, since Congress made finality, not amount in controversy, the criterion for appeal. A fuller factual inquiry would be administratively costly and invite repeated interruption of the trial process.

Section 1292(b) already supplies a limited discretionary path requiring district-judge certification and appellate permission, which the death-knell doctrine would bypass. The doctrine also favors plaintiffs alone, although granting certification can pressure a defendant to settle despite a meritorious defense. Choosing which pressures warrant immediate review is a matter of legislative policy. The Court also rejected broad reliance on Gillespie.

The brief says the casebook's excerpt accurately quotes the three collateral-order failures, and that its later editorial sentence about Rule 23(f) concerns a later permissive-review mechanism that was not part of this 1978 decision.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-501:
The Court began with the policy against piecemeal review but said finality requires a practical assessment of what the district court actually decided. The parties' shared wish for immediate review could not confer jurisdiction. Three features mattered. First, the district court had disposed of the entire complaint and granted the substantive relief sought; the remaining plan was subordinate to issues already determined, and review now would settle the basic issue. Second, delay could obstruct the remedy: divestiture involves extended negotiations dependent on market conditions, which are harder while the underlying duty remains open to appellate invalidation. Third, the Court had repeatedly decided comparable Government antitrust appeals before divestiture was implemented; that practice did not conclusively settle jurisdiction but supported the reading.

On the merits, section 7 asks about reasonable probabilities of substantially lessened competition, and the 1950 amendments reach vertical acquisitions and aim at anticompetitive tendencies before they harden. The vertical merger threatened to foreclose other manufacturers from Kinney as an outlet, given Brown's history of retail acquisitions and the beginning substitution of Brown shoes. The Court also upheld findings of harm to retail competition in cities of at least 10,000 where both firms operated.

Justice Harlan, dissenting on jurisdiction, thought a divestiture plan can determine substantial rights and generate a second appeal, and that the Expediting Act contemplated one appeal after adjudication was complete; on the merits he found the vertical evidence sufficient without endorsing the horizontal analysis. Justice Clark preferred a single national market but found the evidence supported affirmance.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-505:
Mandamus traditionally confines a lower court to its lawful authority or compels it to exercise authority it has a duty to exercise. It is reserved for exceptional circumstances involving judicial usurpation, and the petitioner must show a clear and indisputable entitlement. Disagreement with the correctness of an interlocutory ruling is not enough; otherwise mandamus would displace the congressional policy against piecemeal appeals. A court ordinarily has authority to decide a matter incorrectly, and calling an alleged error a matter of "power" cannot manufacture the conditions for a writ.

Restraint matters especially in criminal cases, where interlocutory review delays trial and government appeals are constrained. The Court assumed that the government had no other avenue of review, but held that this does not authorize appellate courts to supply review Congress has withheld. It reserved whether a dismissal, if entered, would be appealable.

On this record, Rule 7(f) gave the judge substantial discretion over bills of particulars, and a bill may identify some potential witnesses without becoming an impermissible witness-list order. The judge's narrowing of request 25 and rejection of request 29 did not show systematic defiance of governing rules; a liberal approach to discovery and an erroneous ruling, if there was one, are not deliberate disregard of established authority. The Seventh Circuit's lack of any explanation was consequential, because mandamus is corrective and its instructional purpose cannot be served by an unexplained command.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-506:
Mandamus is reserved for exceptional circumstances amounting to a judicial usurpation of power, although jurisdiction is not confined to its narrowest technical meaning. A petitioner must lack other adequate means of obtaining relief and show a clear and indisputable right to the writ, and issuance remains largely discretionary. These restrictions keep mandamus from becoming a routine substitute for interlocutory appeal; frequent extraordinary-writ review would undermine Congress's general decision to postpone appellate review until final judgment, promote piecemeal litigation, and could make the district judge personally defend the challenged action.

Applying those rules, the Court read the Ninth Circuit's Authority-file opinion as keeping renewed privilege assertions and in camera inspection available, not as a final determination that every requested document must be disclosed. A responsible official who had examined the documents could identify a particular record or class and explain the claimed protection. The asserted harms deserved serious consideration: disclosure could chill candid communications within the prison and parole system, expose confidential sources, or compromise sensitive files. Because the weight of confidentiality depended on each document's nature, in camera inspection was a useful, relatively inexpensive way to balance the plaintiffs' needs against the objections, and the Court was confident a proper application could obtain it. Although the second appellate order gave no reasons, the Court saw no basis to conclude it barred the same opportunity for the prisoner files.

The casebook uses the case for the availability of a less drastic avenue for relief and resistance to piecemeal review; the brief notes that the casebook's reference to prisoner personnel files compresses a two-category dispute.
