The Court first rejected the timing objections. Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)'s deadline governs notices of appeal, not petitions under the All Writs Act, and laches did not bar the petition because the Government had actively sought less drastic relief; a party should not be penalized for pursuing alternatives when mandamus requires showing that alternatives are unavailable.

Mandamus remains extraordinary. The petitioner must have no other adequate means of obtaining the desired relief, must establish a clear and indisputable entitlement, and must persuade the issuing court that the writ is appropriate in the circumstances. Here those conditions had to be evaluated with sensitivity to the separation of powers, because the Vice President and senior officials advising the President were the targets of discovery.

Nixon concerned specifically identified evidence needed in an ongoing criminal prosecution. This civil suit sought information to determine whether a statutory duty existed at all, and civil discovery lacked the same criminal-process filters. The requests would have compelled production of the materials the plaintiffs sought as final relief, and more. Requiring the Executive to examine and log the entire mass of material and then invoke privilege document by document could itself create the institutional burden. Executive privilege is a consequential constitutional claim, not a routine step courts must always force before considering narrower ways to resolve a dispute.

Justice Stevens concurred, thinking the discovery order should have been vacated but joining the remand. Justice Thomas, joined by Justice Scalia, would have required the court of appeals to issue the writ. Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justice Souter, dissented and would have affirmed because the Government sought protection from all discovery rather than a narrower plan.

The casebook uses the case for the three mandamus requirements and the privilege-precondition error; the brief notes that the casebook says the Court reversed, when it vacated and remanded.

The Court first rejected the timing objections. Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)'s deadline governs notices of appeal, not petitions under the All Writs Act, and laches did not bar the petition because the Government had actively sought less drastic relief; a party should not be penalized for pursuing alternatives when mandamus requires showing that alternatives are unavailable.

Mandamus remains extraordinary. The petitioner must have no other adequate means of obtaining the desired relief, must establish a clear and indisputable entitlement, and must persuade the issuing court that the writ is appropriate in the circumstances. Here those conditions had to be evaluated with sensitivity to the separation of powers, because the Vice President and senior officials advising the President were the targets of discovery.

Nixon concerned specifically identified evidence needed in an ongoing criminal prosecution. This civil suit sought information to determine whether a statutory duty existed at all, and civil discovery lacked the same criminal-process filters. The requests would have compelled production of the materials the plaintiffs sought as final relief, and more. Requiring the Executive to examine and log the entire mass of material and then invoke privilege document by document could itself create the institutional burden. Executive privilege is a consequential constitutional claim, not a routine step courts must always force before considering narrower ways to resolve a dispute.

Justice Stevens concurred, thinking the discovery order should have been vacated but joining the remand. Justice Thomas, joined by Justice Scalia, would have required the court of appeals to issue the writ. Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justice Souter, dissented and would have affirmed because the Government sought protection from all discovery rather than a narrower plan.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-510:
Section 1292(b) requires the district judge to identify a controlling legal question, substantial grounds for disagreement, and the possibility that immediate review would materially advance termination of the litigation. But its operative language authorizes an appeal from the order, not merely from the judge's selected question. The appellate court may therefore decide an issue fairly included within the certified order, though it may not use the appeal to review other orders in the case. The Court treated the displacement issue as fairly included without separately explaining why; that issue concerned the premise of the very order limiting damages to a federal maritime remedy.

On the merits, admiralty jurisdiction brings in substantive maritime law but does not automatically displace state law. After The Harrisburg refused to recognize a general maritime wrongful-death action, admiralty courts applied state wrongful-death statutes to deaths in territorial waters, so state supplementation had a longstanding place. Moragne overruled The Harrisburg to remove anomalies created by the unseaworthiness doctrine and to extend relief. Its uniformity concern was access to maritime liability principles, not limiting generous state damages for nonseafarers, and it showed no hostility to concurrent state statutes. Congress had not prescribed wrongful-death remedies for nonseafarers in territorial waters, and the Death on the High Seas Act expressly protected state death statutes from displacement by that Act. The Court assumed without deciding that Moragne's action extended to nonseafarers and included a survival action.

The brief says the casebook uses the case for the distinction between the certified order and the certified question, and the restriction to issues fairly included in the order.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-513: The district court dismissed Barry on the ground that his treatment of Smith was not action under color of state law. After a 1988 trial with appointed counsel, the court directed verdicts for several defendants, and the jury found the two psychologists deliberately indifferent to Smith's medical needs and awarded $15,000. The psychologists timely moved for judgment notwithstanding the verdict, which the district court denied on April 13, 1988. The Fourth Circuit, after appointing appellate counsel, dismissed Smith's appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that an informal brief could not be the functional equivalent of a notice of appeal. The Court reversed and remanded. The brief covers only the Court's decision, not the Fourth Circuit's later decision on remand.

Rule 3(c) required a notice to identify the appealing parties, the judgment or order appealed, and the court to which the appeal was taken. The Court treated compliance as jurisdictional but distinguished compliance in substance from adherence to a particular form: liberal construction can recognize a filing that performs the required function, though it cannot excuse the absence of what the rule requires.

The Fourth Circuit's focus on why Smith completed the informal brief asked the wrong question. What matters is the notice the document gives the other parties and the courts, not the filer's subjective motivation, so a timely document supplying the required notice can qualify even though it was submitted in response to briefing instructions.

That a notice ordinarily precedes a brief does not mean one paper can never do both jobs. Rule 3(c) expressly protects an appeal against dismissal for informality of form or title. The appellate court can then require a further document meeting its briefing standards; proper briefing is not a jurisdictional condition.

To the objection that Smith filed in the wrong court, the Court answered that Rule 4(a)(1) provides that a notice mistakenly filed in the court of appeals is deemed filed in the district court on the date of receipt. Whether the brief contained the required information was left for remand.

Justice Scalia relied on Rule 3(c)'s express prohibition on dismissal for informality of form or title, declining to rely on functional equivalence under liberal construction.

The brief says the casebook accurately presents the Court's rejection of a categorical bar and then turns to the 1993 Fourth Circuit remand decision, which is a separate procedural stage.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-514:
Rule 3(c) required the notice to specify the party or parties taking the appeal. Its 1979 amendment protected notices against dismissal for informality of form or title, but the majority distinguished imperfect form from the complete absence of an appeal by a particular party.

Rule 2 permitted suspension of the appellate rules for good cause, subject to Rule 26(b), which barred enlarging the time to file a notice of appeal. Allowing an unnamed party to become an appellant after that period would effectively extend the time to appeal, so the rules withheld both powers. The Advisory Committee's discussion of Rules 3 and 4 supported that reading.

Substantial compliance still has a role: a court may recognize a filing that performs the function of a notice, as in Foman, but may not excuse actual noncompliance, even for good cause. Torres was never designated, even inartfully. "Et al." did not tell the employer or the court which unnamed persons intended to appeal, which also affects who would be bound by an adverse judgment and liable for costs or sanctions. The Court acknowledged the result was harsh. Harmless-error relief was unavailable because failure to clear a jurisdictional threshold cannot be harmless or waived.

Justice Scalia concurred in the judgment, reading the specification requirement strictly according to its apparent intent rather than under liberal construction. Justice Brennan dissented: he would have reversed and remanded for a factual inquiry into whether the notice actually communicated Torres's intent to appeal, distinguishing Rule 4's timing requirement from Rule 3(c)'s content requirement.

The brief says the casebook gives the omitted-name, clerical-error and "et al." account, and that its due-process question is an editorial prompt rather than a holding of the Court.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-516:
Budinich argued that Colorado law controlled finality and that applying section 1291 would violate the Tenth Amendment. The Court rejected both points: state law supplies rules of decision in diversity cases but does not displace a governing federal statute, and Congress's regulation of appeals between federal courts is procedural and necessary and proper to its authority to establish those courts.

A final decision is one that ends the litigation on the merits and leaves only execution of the judgment. An unresolved matter does not defeat finality if its resolution cannot alter the merits order or moot or revise decisions embodied in it. Earlier decisions, including White, had treated fees as collateral to the merits. The Court acknowledged that simply calling fees collateral assumes the answer where a party claims the fees are part of the merits. Generally, fees do not remedy the underlying injury, may be awarded to a defending party, and have traditionally been treated as costs.

Budinich's stronger argument was that the authorizing law can make fees part of the merits. The Court concluded that the characterization chosen by the underlying law should not control. Finality concerns the functioning of the judicial system: whether a statute deems fees part of the merits does not make a merits appeal more disruptive. A rule that depended on characterization would force parties to resolve a difficult classification question before knowing when their jurisdictional appeal clock began. A uniform rule gives clearer, more predictable timing.

The Court also refused prospective-only application, because an untimely merits appeal gave the court of appeals no authority to review the merits.

The brief says the casebook presents the dates and quotes the bright-line rationale, and that its statement that the Court dismissed all issues except fees compresses what the Tenth Circuit did and what the Court affirmed.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-517:
Section 2107(a) sets the ordinary thirty-day civil appeal period, and section 2107(c) authorizes limited reopening for fourteen additional days when specified conditions are met; Rule 4 implements that statute. The defect was that the reopening order itself purported to allow more than fourteen days.

The majority relied on longstanding treatment of statutory civil appellate deadlines as mandatory and jurisdictional. It distinguished recent decisions cautioning against loose use of the word "jurisdictional": in Kontrick the deadline came from a bankruptcy rule rather than a statute, and only Congress can define the lower federal courts' jurisdiction. The Court's own certiorari deadlines show the same line, with a statute-based civil deadline treated as jurisdictional and a rule-based criminal one open to relaxation. Because Congress decides whether and under what time conditions federal courts may hear a class of cases, the limit was more than a claim-processing rule, and forfeiture or waiver could not cure noncompliance.

Bowles invoked the unique-circumstances doctrine of Harris Truck Lines and Thompson, which had protected litigants who relied on a district court's mistaken assurance. Because the Court has no power to create equitable exceptions to jurisdictional requirements, it overruled those cases to the extent they purported to authorize such an exception. Congress could authorize rules excusing compliance, but had not done so here.

Justice Souter, joined by Justices Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer, dissented. He argued that a deadline is not jurisdictional merely because it appears in a statute, that the majority's approach was inconsistent with recent unanimous efforts to separate claim-processing rules from true jurisdictional limits, and that reliance on the judge's order was reasonable and should be protected. He would have vacated and remanded for consideration of the merits.

The brief says the casebook recounts the late notice filed in conformity with the mistaken order and then compares the later Hamer decision, which is textbook commentary.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-520:
"Neglect" in its ordinary meaning encompasses carelessness as well as some omissions without fault, so a categorical rule limited to outside forces would disregard that meaning. That the rule can reach inadvertence, mistake or negligence does not mean every such omission is excusable. The Chapter 11 setting, which aims at rehabilitation and avoiding unnecessary forfeiture, reinforced this reading. The Court also drew on similar language in Civil Rule 6(b) and, as to Rule 60(b), emphasized that subsections (1) and (6) are mutually exclusive.

The majority identified four principal considerations: the danger of prejudice to the debtor; the length of the delay and its potential impact on the proceedings; the reason for the delay, including whether it was within the movant's reasonable control; and whether the movant acted in good faith. These are relevant circumstances, not a mechanical formula.

A represented party cannot avoid the acts and omissions of its freely selected agent; relying on Link and Boyle, the Court asked whether the neglect of both the creditors and their counsel was excusable. The unchallenged findings of good faith, no prejudice and no administrative disruption strongly favored relief. The Court gave little weight to counsel's professional upheaval but treated the unusual notice as significant, because a bar date would ordinarily be prominent and explained. Had there been evidence of prejudice, disruption or bad faith, the Court said it could not have found the bankruptcy court's refusal an abuse of discretion.

Justice O'Connor, joined by Justices Scalia, Souter and Thomas, dissented. She read the rule as requiring first that the neglect itself be excusable in cause and culpability, and only then an exercise of discretion in light of the equities, and would have upheld the denial.

The brief says the casebook cites the case for the late bankruptcy claim and the four-factor analysis, and separately quotes its treatment of negligent omissions under Rules 6 and 60 in the Briones passage.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-524:
The majority distinguished claim preclusion from issue preclusion. The counterclaims asserted a right not previously adjudicated as a cause of action, so claim preclusion did not apply; but a matter actually litigated and essential to a final judgment can bind the parties in a different cause of action. An immaterial finding would have no preclusive effect.

The separate-trial order did not guarantee a second chance to prove conspiracy. A trial court may modify such an order before final judgment, and Partmar had an opportunity to present evidence and contest the finding, including argument before the findings were adopted. A second trial on a conclusively determined issue would defeat preclusion, and the dismissal did not deny due process.

On appeal rights, the majority said in a footnote that Partmar could have appealed the determination. Findings unnecessary to a decree neither support an appeal by a prevailing party nor establish preclusion, but the no-conspiracy finding was necessary to defeating Paramount's possession claim.

The majority also rejected Partmar's reliance on the government antitrust judgment as prima facie evidence under section 5 of the Clayton Act: the final Paramount decree contained no finding that these particular agreements resulted from the industry conspiracy.

Chief Justice Warren, joined by Justice Black, dissented. In his view Partmar's conspiracy defense had been stricken, the parties had consented to separate trials, and the judge acknowledged that no evidence had been offered on the counterclaims, so the issue was not actually litigated. He also disputed that Partmar could have appealed a finding in a case it won, and reasoned that if it could not appeal the finding it should not be bound by it. Justices Jackson and Clark did not participate.

The brief says the casebook uses the case for the disagreement over whether a party that won the original claim but lost on its counterclaim may appeal an issue directly affecting the latter, and that the footnote's emphasis is narrower, turning on the finding's necessity to the decree.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-538:
On joinder, Vanover failed to show under Rule 19(a) that she could not obtain complete monetary relief from NCO without the additional companies; a bare parent-subsidiary relationship and unsupported assertions that the parent directed NCO did not establish the necessary liability or control. Rule 20(a) generally encourages joinder, but the district court could consider practical fairness and docket management. The additions were proposed to defeat the claim-splitting motion and exposed NCO to further duplicative litigation and possible inconsistent outcomes, and NCO had no obligation to seek consolidation to repair her litigation choices.

On claim-splitting, actual finality of the first action is unnecessary because the doctrine manages pending duplicative cases; ordinary claim preclusion's protection of final judgments is related but distinct. The test examines the same parties or their privies and the same transaction or series of transactions, with a shared nucleus of operative facts evaluated pragmatically through time, origin, motivation, convenient trial unit, and party expectations. Here the parties were identical after joinder was denied, and both cases challenged the same collection efforts on the same medical accounts. Extending the period backward, adding other telephones and third-party contacts, or labeling the conduct under additional statutes did not create an independent transaction.

The casebook uses the case for the two-part inquiry and the lack of a final-judgment requirement; the brief notes that the casebook's account omits the additional statutory theories and the joinder appeal.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-550:
The Court distinguished two situations. When a later suit concerns the same claim or demand, a merits judgment bars the subsequent action. When the later suit concerns a different demand, the inquiry is whether the particular point presented was actually litigated and determined in the earlier action. The opinion uses the historical term res judicata for both; the brief explains that the second branch is what is now called issue preclusion. These suits fell within the second branch, because the installments differed but the status question was the same.

The Court accepted a limited qualification to the Government's law-versus-fact argument. An unmixed legal rule announced in one case does not bind the same parties in a suit on a different demand merely because they were parties to the first case. But a distinctly adjudged fact, question, or right cannot be disputed again between them simply by alleging an erroneous legal view or application. Otherwise a court would nominally honor the adjudicated matter while defeating its conclusive effect through an attack on its supporting reasoning. An individual's status on which recovery depends is as conclusive as any other adjudicated matter. Conclusiveness is tied to the right, question, or fact put in issue and directly determined, with the prior judgment unmodified and the relevant circumstances identical. No separate opinion is reported.

The casebook uses the case, under the heading of defining and characterizing the issue, for the distinction between an unmixed legal rule and a distinctly adjudicated right or status.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-585:
The Anti-Injunction Act ordinarily forbids federal injunctions staying state proceedings but excepts injunctions necessary to protect or effectuate federal judgments. The Court read that exception consistently with section 1738 rather than as an implied partial repeal of it. Before the state court rules on a federal-judgment preclusion defense, the relitigation exception may permit protective relief in an appropriate case; after the state court has finally rejected the defense, section 1738 controls.

The Eleventh Circuit relied on Congress's 1948 response to Toucey, but the parties in Toucey had gone to federal court before the state courts resolved the preclusion question. Here the bank chose to litigate that question in state court and returned to federal court only after losing. Inefficient parallel litigation did not justify the injunction, since concurrent proceedings are part of the dual system. Even a mistaken state preclusion ruling does not, merely because it is mistaken, justify a federal injunction; correction ordinarily comes through state appeals and potential Supreme Court review.

The Court did not decide that the state ruling was preclusive under Alabama law. If the District Court found it was not, it could then consider an injunction under general principles of equity, comity, and federalism. The Court left open whether the relitigation exception protects claims that could have been but were not litigated in the federal action, and whether the trustee was bound.

The casebook note describes the Alabama ruling as an appeals court ruling that mistakenly rejected the defense; the brief notes that the Court placed the ruling in the state trial proceedings and did not decide whether it was wrong.

CP-COMP-CB-CAP-591:
The Arbitration Act ordinarily supported enforcement and a stay, and the Court recognized Congress's aim of overcoming judicial hostility to arbitration. But the Securities Act addressed buyers' informational disadvantages, and the Court had to accommodate both policies. Section 12(2) gave purchasers a special civil remedy, and section 22 broadened the available forums with advantageous venue and service rules; the Court treated these procedural protections as part of the statutory design.

The Court accepted that arbitrators would have to apply the Securities Act, so the objection was not that the contract formally erased substantive rights. It looked to their practical effectiveness. Before a controversy arose the buyer could not adequately assess the disadvantages of giving up the choice of courts, and Congress had legislated for investors' unequal access to information. Determining materiality, knowledge, reasonable care, and the burden of proof required legal judgments, yet arbitrators could decide without judicial instruction, without stating reasons, and without a complete record. The Arbitration Act's vacatur grounds were limited, and ordinary errors of legal interpretation, as distinct from manifest disregard, were not reviewable. The Court drew an analogy to Boyd v. Grand Trunk Western Railroad, which invalidated a restriction on an employee's statutory choice of venue.

Justice Jackson agreed but thought parties could agree to arbitrate after a controversy arose, and declined to endorse any conclusion about review of an actual award. Justice Frankfurter argued that the record did not show arbitration would deny the statutory protections or that Wilko had no practical choice, and would have affirmed.

The casebook quotes the Court's accommodation of arbitration policy and investor protection in a section on changing judicial attitudes; the brief states the historical 1953 decision and does not certify it as current law.

CP-COMP-CB-HAEGER-REMAND:
Applying Arizona agency principles, the court treated a principal as responsible for acts undertaken by its agents within the scope of their work and in furtherance of the principal's business. The attorney-client relationship did not make Goodyear a passive stranger to the misconduct: its associate general counsel approved discovery decisions, knew of the bad-faith conduct and took part in the concealment, and earlier findings established Goodyear's direct involvement.

Because the plaintiffs had settled with Musnuff and Fennemore Craig and represented that their participation was unnecessary, the court excused the lawyers once Goodyear was held responsible.

On waiver, the court separated two issues. One was the governing legal measure: incremental fees caused by wrongdoing rather than all fees incurred after a particular point. The other was which specific billing entries failed that measure. Goodyear preserved the first, but that did not automatically preserve entry-specific objections it had never presented. Its own detailed coding showed it knew how to identify causation objections; the court had warned of the alternative award and invited guidance; Goodyear offered nothing more and received every deduction it sought. The additional challenges first appeared on appeal, and the court applied the ordinary rule against considering arguments first raised there, finding persuasive the distinction emphasized in Judge M. Smith's earlier dissent. Winning the legal standard in the Supreme Court did not entitle Goodyear to redo objections it could have made, which would reward strategic withholding.

The casebook cites the order for the remand determinations of waiver and vicarious responsibility; the brief notes that the casebook's reference to an alternative $2 million award is shorthand, since the order left the remaining amount for further proceedings.

CP-COMP-CB-INSET:
The plaintiff had to make a prima facie showing, and the inquiry had two separate steps: the long-arm statute and due process.

On the statute, section 33-411(c)(2) subjected a foreign corporation to a resident's suit arising from business repeatedly solicited in the state. ISI did not specifically contest it. Earlier district decisions had found repeated solicitation in advertisements in publications circulated in Connecticut, and the court treated continuous Internet advertising as at least sufficiently repetitive, since users in the state could access the same advertisement repeatedly, with greater reach than discarded printed materials. The court did not require evidence of completed Connecticut sales.

On due process, ISI argued that its Massachusetts base and lack of Connecticut presence defeated minimum contacts. The court applied purposeful availment and reasonable anticipation of litigation, and inferred that ISI directed its online advertising and telephone number toward every state, including Connecticut; nationwide reach did not exclude purposeful direction to this state. Jurisdiction was also fair given the minimal distance from Massachusetts, Connecticut's interest in its own common-law and statutory claims, and efficient resolution. ISI had not developed a distinct fairness objection.

On venue, the then-applicable section 1391(b)(1) permitted suit where a defendant resided, and section 1391(c) deemed a corporate defendant resident where it was subject to personal jurisdiction when the action began.

The casebook presents Inset as an early Internet-jurisdiction decision; the brief treats its reasoning as historical and not as a current rule that every accessible website establishes jurisdiction everywhere.

On appealability, the court looked to the order's legal effect rather than its label; otherwise destruction of the class action would evade review.

Section 382 reflects equity's doctrine of representative litigation, and precedent required both an ascertainable class and a well-defined community of interest. Identifying every member at the outset is different from showing an ascertainable class; an inability presently to name all people affected by common issues does not foreclose a representative suit, and a later claimant would still have to identify himself and establish his entitlement.

The court rejected Yellow Cab's argument that community must extend to common relief. No common fund or single indivisible recovery is required; individual calculations can be subsidiary to common questions. What matters is whether numerous substantial individual questions would remain. The court distinguished cases where each person's right to recover depended on unique facts from cases where basic liability questions were shared and amounts could be determined mathematically. The 1966 revision of federal Rule 23 was a useful comparison but not controlling.

Applied to the complaint, both groups faced a uniform overcharge from the same pricing practice, and an accounting could establish amounts from company records. Separate actions would likely cost more than each rider could recover, and without a class procedure Yellow Cab might retain the benefits of the alleged wrongdoing. The court declined judicial notice of fare structures and tipping practices offered to discredit the uniform-overcharge allegation, because they were not beyond reasonable dispute.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-125:
Mississippi law controlled, and the court had to decide as a Mississippi court would, considering prior holdings and later indications from the state's highest court. In Ford Motor Co. v. Myers, Mississippi had declined to follow MacPherson. But in E. I. Du Pont de Nemours & Co. v. Ladner the Mississippi Supreme Court, while resolving the case on causation, deliberately and approvingly discussed the modern principle allowing remote consumers to recover for a manufacturer's negligence. The First Circuit's Mason decision had read that discussion, with the overwhelming modern trend, as signaling abandonment of Ford's rule, and this court agreed, acknowledging that it was unusual to prefer recent considered dicta to an older contrary holding.

Negligence was in the case: the complaint alleged contamination when the product was manufactured, packaged and sealed, counsel argued negligent packaging, and Grey requested a res ipsa instruction. Sealed-container contamination could support res ipsa under Mississippi principles, subject to the plaintiff's burden.

On warranty, the overall sales relationship made Quinn a selling agent despite the agreement's terminology, so privity was satisfied through agency, not abolished. Disclaimers must clearly identify the warranties excluded and are construed against the seller; this clause addressed hazards of using the described insecticide, not an undisclosed foreign herbicide. On causation, residue from the brother's use should have diminished after the first drumload, so uniform severe damage across two loads supported an inference that the second can replenished the herbicide. A new trial would serve no useful purpose.

The casebook uses Grey to illustrate state-law prediction after Mason; the brief notes that its statement that lack of privity did not bar the claim compresses the two distinct routes.

CP-COMP-CB-LOWER-224:
Cy pres permits an indirect, next-best use of settlement funds that are unclaimed or impracticable to distribute, but a good charitable purpose is not enough. The distribution must be guided by the underlying statutory objectives and the absent class members' interests, including the class's geographic reach; without that nexus the choice may serve the preferences of the parties, lawyers or court and create an appearance of impropriety. Under Six Mexican Workers, a distribution must address the statutory objectives, target the plaintiff class, and give reasonable certainty that members will benefit.

These donations failed. The recipients had no demonstrated connection to the electronic-communications and commercial-email interests underlying the claims. Two-thirds of the principal donations went to local Los Angeles charities despite a nationwide class, and the Federal Judicial Center Foundation, though national, had no apparent connection to the statutory purposes. AOL's plea for deference to the settlement as fair, reasonable and adequate confused two inquiries: the adequacy of the settlement as a whole and the validity of its distribution. The standards apply whether the parties or the judge select recipients, and a mediator's involvement does not remove the nexus requirement. Suitable beneficiaries were not impossible to find, since all members used the internet; organizations protecting internet users from online fraud were plausible. If none could be identified, the district court should consider escheat to the Treasury.

On recusal, a reasonable informed observer would not necessarily question the judge's impartiality merely from her husband's volunteer board membership, and Legal Aid was not a party; remote or speculative benefits did not create a disqualifying interest.

The casebook cites the case for the nexus failure; the brief notes that the footers were appended to subscribers' outgoing messages and that the wrongdoing was alleged, not adjudicated.

CP-COMP-CB-RANDONE:
The court rejected the agency's reading of Sniadach as limited to wages. Its recent Blair v. Pitchess decision had applied the same reasoning to claim and delivery, and federal and California decisions reflected a general requirement of an opportunity to be heard before a significant deprivation, subject to exceptional countervailing interests. The property interest at stake was use of the property before judgment; calling attachment temporary did not remove that interest or the hardship of losing it.

Summary action can be justified, as in banking and public-health cases involving urgent public protection and tailored statutes. Section 537(1) lacked that tailoring: it made security available broadly without proof that delay would frustrate collection. The agency's claim that attachment was essential to available credit was unsupported on the record. An actual danger of flight or concealment could support a carefully limited summary remedy, but the statute required no particularized showing and none was made here.

The statute also reached necessities. Bank funds needed by an unemployed family could be as vital as wages, and the creditor's power to choose the property allowed the greatest settlement pressure. Such deprivation could undermine the later hearing itself by forcing a debtor to settle even a meritorious defense. A creditor's private security interest did not justify taking necessities before a hearing on the validity of the claim, and post-attachment exemptions did not cure the problem.

The court contemplated a valid scheme protecting necessities, ordinarily permitting attachment after notice and a hearing on probable validity, with safeguarded exceptions for demonstrated risk of concealment or flight.

The casebook cites the case in its attachment note as the decision invalidating the summary attachment statute; its description of later legislation is editorial context.

CP-COMP-CB-REF-180:
Rule 23(c)(2)(B) requires individual notice to all members identifiable through reasonable effort. The court assumed the Rice declaration was admissible; even so, the refusal to require any search could not stand.

The court distinguished finding recipients from paying to deliver notice. Eisen treated individual notice to reasonably identifiable members as mandatory, not dispensable because of expense. Oppenheimer addressed who bears identification costs and did not eliminate the need to obtain available identifying information. Expense, anticipated results and the amount involved inform reasonable effort, but size alone does not excuse effort, because a large class may require a large search. Domestic Air involved a list whose relationship to class membership was highly uncertain, whereas Sprint acknowledged its records could identify millions of actual members. An accurate partial list requires notice even when a complete one is impracticable. The district court had originally recognized that, then changed course with little explanation.

The costs reinforced the point: if the $100,000 search identified two million members, identification would cost about five cents each, or about forty-three cents with mailing. These were hypothetical calculations. The people who had paid the fees stood to receive much of the settlement yet were generally no longer current customers reachable by bill inserts.

On adequacy, Rule 23(a)(4) involves both freedom from conflicts and the ability and incentive to represent the class vigorously. The district court stressed the absence of antagonism but did not adequately examine whether former customers had an incentive to prevent continued fee enforcement against current subscribers, some of whom could receive only Category IV's noncash benefits.

The casebook quotes the court's cost reasoning; the brief notes that the casebook summarizes it as a refusal to order a search, while the opinion left the reasonable-effort decision to the district court on remand.

CP-COMP-CB-ROBINSON-MEYER:
The court found the result plainly just but still examined whether the plaintiffs' procedural objection required a new trial. The defendants' amended answer alleged facts adequate to establish adverse possession if continued for the requisite time. The plaintiffs denied that allegation in open court, considerable evidence on use and occupation was introduced, and the court's examination of the record confirmed that the facts underlying the defense were actually litigated.

Those same pleaded facts established the ouster that invalidated Hastings's 1934 deed. The trial court therefore was not deciding on an unpleaded factual basis; it supplied the legal effect of facts already put in issue. Naming the statute might have clarified the defense, but its omission did not prevent the court from applying it. Because the plaintiffs had joined issue on the underlying question, applying the statute caused no procedural injustice warranting a new trial. The opinion cited other Connecticut cases applying statutory consequences in comparable circumstances.

The court did not find that the full fifteen-year adverse-possession period had run. The occupation's potential to ripen into title explained the character of the possession, while the statutory ouster invalidated an intervening deed.

The casebook describes the case as an inference of adverse-possession title from facts establishing ouster; the brief notes that this compresses the actual mechanism, which was that Hastings's deed was void under the ouster statute, and that the case illustrates how a court may supply legal consequences to adequately pleaded facts.

CP-COMP-CB-SMITH-BARRY-REMAND:
Rule 3(c), as applied in the opinion, required specification of the appealing party, designation of the judgment or order challenged, and identification of the appellate court. The Court's mandate required liberal construction of papers supplying the functional equivalent of those requirements but did not authorize ignoring actual noncompliance. The panel declined to base jurisdiction on the defective March notice and looked only to the timely informal brief.

As to the guards, the deliberate-indifference claim against them had been tried before a jury and ended in a directed verdict. Read in that procedural setting, a request for a new trial on jury issues supplied the necessary designation even without their names or a reference to the February 29 order. This was contextual substantial compliance, not a rule that a general new-trial request always suffices.

Barry's position differed. His dismissal came on a legal motion years before trial, and the brief neither mentioned him nor identified that order; asking for a new jury trial did not communicate a challenge to a pretrial legal dismissal, and liberal reading could not turn the paper into notice of that different appeal. The court did not affirm Barry's dismissal on its state-action rationale.

On the merits, viewing the evidence and reasonable inferences in Smith's favor, he offered no evidence that the six guards could meaningfully address his medical needs. Medical staff handled those needs, and the jury had found two members of that staff liable.

CP-COMP-CB-TRIPLE-UP-DISTRICT: Triple Up filed suit in the District Court for the District of Columbia on February 1, 2016, asserting copyright public-performance and reproduction and distribution theories, direct and secondary liability, a Lanham Act claim, and common-law unfair competition; certain additional theories had been withdrawn. The court granted the Rule 12(b)(2) motion and dismissed the action, denied jurisdictional discovery, and denied the alternative Rule 12(b)(6) motion as moot. This entry covers the district decision only; the later appellate affirmance is a distinct stage.

Triple Up filed suit in the District Court for the District of Columbia on February 1, 2016, asserting copyright public-performance and reproduction and distribution theories, direct and secondary liability, a Lanham Act claim, and common-law unfair competition; certain additional theories had been withdrawn. Youku moved under Rule 12(b)(2) and alternatively Rule 12(b)(6). The court granted the Rule 12(b)(2) motion and dismissed the action, denied jurisdictional discovery, and denied the alternative Rule 12(b)(6) motion as moot. The court of appeals later affirmed.

A globally accessible website did not itself establish purposeful American activity. Triple Up's novel argument was that Youku's ability to exclude American viewers made its failure to do so a deliberate decision to serve them. The court rejected that inference on this record: purposeful availment ordinarily requires affirmative conduct directed toward a forum, not merely failure to prevent access from it. Otherwise any website operator capable of filtering locations could be sued everywhere it did not block. The court did not say geoblocking could never matter in a future case.

On advertising, the judge avoided deciding whether hosting English-language, geographically targeted advertisements amounted to purposeful availment. Even assuming it did, the claims failed the separate relatedness requirement, which the court read as requiring at least some causal connection: removing the advertisements would leave the asserted infringement unchanged. The brief notes this is the court's 2017 relatedness analysis.

The ability to register accounts, search and watch videos did not establish claim-related forum transactions, and the stock-exchange listing and contracts with American advertising agencies, software providers and content producers had no connection with the films. Triple Up waived an effects-test argument under Calder by not presenting it, and the court observed that no American business injury was alleged by this Seychelles plaintiff.

Discovery was denied because most of the seven requested categories concerned contacts already found unrelated to the claims. On servers, the court accepted that claim-related American operations might matter, but Triple Up offered only a hunch; discovery requires a plausible factual lead.

The casebook uses the dispute to test whether technological control over access amounts to forum targeting.

CP-COMP-CB-TWIN-FLAMES:
The plaintiffs bore the burden and, on an affidavit-based motion, had to offer reasonably particular facts; the court construed the facts in their favor. It treated Michigan's long-arm reach as coextensive with due process and applied the circuit's specific-jurisdiction requirements.

Knowledge of the plaintiffs' location was insufficient. Calder permitted jurisdiction where the publication had a developed forum focus, including local sources and substantial circulation, while Walden requires the defendant's own meaningful connection with the forum, not one supplied only by the plaintiff's residence or injury. The court also relied on the Sixth Circuit's Blessing decision on social-media criticism.

The Canadian interview showed no Michigan targeting. The plaintiffs offered no evidence of Vice Media's Michigan circulation or intended Michigan audience, and the article's Michigan references were made by the reporter and unnamed parents, not Cole. The subreddit posts concerned the business generally; neither the board nor Cole's comments identified Michigan, and the plaintiffs showed no effort to reach Michigan readers specifically. A complaint about an Internet business headquartered in the forum is not necessarily aimed at the forum's public. Michigan readers who canceled contracts could not supply Cole's contacts, because third parties' locations and choices do not show that she created forum contacts.

On transfer, the judge recognized authority to transfer in the interests of justice despite missing personal jurisdiction, discussing §§ 1631 and 1406(a). But the cease-and-desist letter's explicit threat of distant litigation expense supported an inference that the improper forum was chosen to increase Cole's costs. The litigation was in its infancy, and the plaintiffs identified no prejudice or limitations bar. The brief notes that the application paragraph refers to § 1404(a) without explanation.

The casebook uses the case both for its Internet-jurisdiction forum-focus analysis and, in a separate note, for the choice between transfer and dismissal.

CP-COMP-CB-VUITTON:
The historical Rule 65(b) required specific facts showing immediate and irreparable injury before the opponent could be heard, plus counsel's written certification of efforts to give notice and the reasons notice should not be required. The second requirement does not say the opponent must be impossible to reach; it allows a supported explanation that giving notice would itself defeat the preservation the order is meant to accomplish.

The panel acknowledged the general commitment to notice and a chance to be heard. An ex parte order may preserve the status quo and avert irreparable harm only for the time needed to arrange a hearing, and prior circuit warnings insisted on careful compliance with the rule rather than imposing an absolute prohibition. Here the goods' disappearance before a hearing could leave the court unable to give effective relief. The panel found likelihood of confusion, since the items were virtually identical and marketed to induce buyers to believe they were Vuitton goods, and under the trademark doctrine it applied in 1979 that likelihood itself supplied irreparable injury. The affidavit's account of rapid transfers through a poorly documented network explained why notice should be dispensed with in this case.

Mandamus was justified because, without a prompt order or certified interlocutory review, such cases would rarely progress in a form allowing an effective appellate ruling on the notice issue, and district judges' practices differed. The panel treated the issue as capable of repetition yet evading review and characterized the case as extraordinary.

The casebook attributes the no-notice order to the presence of many defendants not yet identified; the brief notes the opinion's reason was more specific, that notice to the named defendants risked transfer of inventory to other, unidentified sellers.

CP-COMP-CB-WASHINGTON-TRUMP:
TROs are ordinarily not appealable, but an order so labeled can be reviewed if it has a preliminary injunction's qualities, which ordinarily requires a substantial adversarial challenge and an order extending beyond Rule 65(b)'s fourteen-day period. Both were present, and given the national-security emergency the Government asserted, that sufficed at this stage. The label did not control, but neither did adversarial participation alone.

On standing, the universities were undisputed branches of the States, so the entry restrictions caused proprietary institutional injury that relief could redress; the universities could also assert the rights of students and faculty. The court left other standing theories unresolved. It rejected the Government's claim that immigration and national-security decisions were unreviewable, distinguishing substantial deference from complete immunity from judicial review.

A stay is discretionary and the Government bore the burden. The court considered likelihood of success, irreparable injury to the applicant, injury to other parties, and the public interest, the first two being most important. Due process protects persons within the United States, including noncitizens, and certain returning noncitizens; the Government had not shown that returning permanent residents lacked rights or that the order supplied sufficient process. The White House counsel guidance did not moot those claims. The court declined to narrow the TRO to fewer persons or to the two States. It reserved the religious-discrimination claims. On irreparable injury, the Government's interest in combating terrorism did not itself explain the need to reinstate the restrictions immediately, while the States showed disrupted university work, separated families and stranded residents.

The casebook uses the decision to illustrate when a TRO functions as a preliminary injunction for appellate review; the brief notes that the casebook's emphasis on vigorous opposition compresses the court's additional reliance on duration and scheduling.

Richard Guilmet experienced nearly fatal bleeding from a peptic ulcer in fall 1963. His treating physician, Dr. Klewicki, recommended Drs. Campbell and Arena. At a January 1964 consultation Guilmet asked whether he should undergo an operation; according to the majority nobody told him he had to, and Campbell testified that Guilmet was in excellent physical condition and that the operation was not an emergency.

The alleged promises came from Guilmet's testimony, not a written guarantee. He said Campbell represented that the operation would remove his troubles, let him eat and drink freely and resume normal activities; that Campbell and Arena were experienced specialists; that the operation was simple and without danger; that hospitalization would be four or five days and absence from work at most three or four weeks; and that he could discard his medication afterward. The trial judge doubted that Campbell made every statement but recognized that the jury could credit Guilmet's account.

Guilmet then had the operation. The majority described a ruptured esophagus associated with surgical trauma during the vagotomy, further operations to insert drainage tubes, hepatitis that Campbell thought probably resulted from transfusions, severe coughing and vomiting, and a decline in weight from 170 to 88 pounds. He could no longer maintain his previous work and recreation. The brief does not fix the operation date because the opinions describe it differently.

Relying on Kemper and Lemoge, the court said that a bid subject to a nonwithdrawal condition, once opened and declared, could function as an irrevocable option that ordinary unilateral withdrawal could not destroy. The bidder could nevertheless rescind if the requirements for equitable relief were met: the mistake must be material and not result from neglect of a legal duty; enforcement must be unconscionable; the other party must be capable of restoration to the status quo; and the mistaken party must promptly elect rescission and restore or offer to restore any value received. Knowledge, or reason to know, of the other party's mistake supported relief rather than a right to exploit it. Ordinary carelessness was not invariably the neglect of legal duty that defeated rescission.

The court found certain trial findings unsupported and others immaterial. The worksheets, which the court inspected itself, and uncontradicted testimony, including from the district's own architect, superintendent, and board member, established the clerical mechanism and the board's receipt of notice. Mere time and opportunity to check did not establish neglect of a legal duty. Kastorff's assurance at bid opening did not bar relief: he had no worksheets then, checked them at the earliest practicable opportunity, and promptly notified the district. The district's August 15 refusal came with knowledge of the asserted error, and the written notification came about two weeks after rescission. The district had no legitimate expectation of plumbing without charge. Whether the omission was $6,500 or $9,285, it was material relative to $89,994. Prompt withdrawal, unlike the performance followed by a reformation request in Lemoge, was central.

The brief notes that the casebook's statement that the court agreed with favorable trial findings about Kastorff is inaccurate, and that the later public-contract statute in the casebook notes was enacted after this decision.

Justice Lowrie began by separating relationships commonly gathered under the label implied contract. A true contract rests on the parties' mutual intention: it is express when the terms are openly stated and implied when actual intention is inferred from circumstances. A constructive contract, by contrast, is a legal fiction used to enforce a duty through a contract remedy even when the parties had no intention to contract; its duty comes from law. The court said this case asserted a proper express or implied agreement, not a constructive obligation, so the quantum-meruit count did not let the jury replace proof of the agreement with a general belief that payment would be fair.

Ordinary work for a stranger may support an inference of hiring because the relationship otherwise calls for an explanation. An existing relationship may supply that explanation, as with neighbors helping to save a burning house. Family association likewise could account for a son's work for his father. A party claiming a contract must prove it, and circumstances equally explained by the family relationship are insufficient. Here the shared household, the father's management, the absence of accounts, and the presumed support supplied the family explanation. Relatives were not incapable of contracting: accounts, periodic wages, or a settlement of wages might show an express contract, but none was present.

The father's statements acknowledged that the son deserved a reward while leaving unproved any existing agreement, and John's repeated unsuccessful requests suggested he wanted an agreement, not that one existed. John's argument on review that the farm was run jointly with profits divided had no evidence behind it.

The casebook note cites the case for its treatment of family services and refusal of restitution; the brief notes that Lowrie identified the theory before him as one requiring a real contract and did not decide every unjust-enrichment theory.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B2-006:
The public contracting statutes did not expressly address a disappointed bidder's damages. The court declined to read that silence as a prohibition, since it could equally reflect an assumption that existing promissory-estoppel principles supplied relief, and found no statutory barrier to a valid equitable theory.

Under Restatement section 90, when a public entity solicits bids it represents, consistently with its statutory obligation, that if it awards the contract the award will go to the lowest responsible bidder, and bid preparation expenses are incurred in reliance on that representation. MTA did not dispute that these circumstances appeared to establish the elements; Kajima conceded it had neither a tort nor a breach-of-contract claim. The fit with ordinary promissory estoppel was imperfect, because the court was chiefly furthering the public policies behind competitive bidding. Earlier decisions denying reimbursement after a valid rejection of all bids were distinguishable as an ordinary risk of pursuing public work.

Preparation costs were reasonably incurred in reliance on fair evaluation. Expected profits were not expenditures incurred in reliance and were uncertain; awarding them could put the bidder in a better position than performance. Public policy independently limited the remedy: competitive bidding primarily protects taxpayers, and paying the higher contractor and also an unperformed contract's profits would compound the public loss. Large profit awards could encourage opportunistic litigation. Rules for ordinary private breach-of-contract damages did not control because Kajima had no contract with MTA. The court surveyed other jurisdictions, many of which allow preparation costs but not profits. Its reasoning does not prohibit lost profits in all private promissory-estoppel actions.

On March 31, 1994, the district court held that it had subject-matter jurisdiction but dismissed Hakimoglu's affirmative claims, predicting that New Jersey would not recognize a dram-shop action for gambling losses. After the Third Circuit's September 6 decision in Greate Bay Hotel & Casino v. Tose, the court invited briefing on reconsideration. The casino separately moved for partial summary judgment on the unpaid markers.

On December 23, 1994, the court denied reconsideration, denied the casino's partial-summary-judgment motion without prejudice, and certified the dismissal for immediate appeal under Rule 54(b). At this district-court stage there was no trial, finding of incapacity, or recovery on the markers.

Sitting in diversity, the court had to predict New Jersey law. New Jersey dram-shop law protected persons injured by negligent alcohol service, but the court found no state authority extending it to gambling losses, which differ from drunken-driving injuries, falls, and fights.

Greate Bay decided only that the Casino Control Commission lacked exclusive primary jurisdiction and expressly reserved whether a cause of action existed; its remark that a reasonable argument could be made for a duty warranted careful consideration, not a change in the law. The court gave several reasons against expanded liability: the patron chooses to gamble; baccarat turns on chance; causation is difficult because sober patrons may lose and intoxicated ones may win; a claim brought years later lacks contemporaneous evidence; and regulation, together with the unenforceability of credit extended to a person lacking capacity, already deters misconduct.

On the markers, the Casino Control Act did not abrogate contract defenses such as incapacity from intoxication, duress, and unconscionability. Equitable estoppel can apply to contracts, but it requires justified and reasonable detrimental reliance by an innocent party. The casino offered no affidavits establishing what it knew about Hakimoglu's drinking and gambling, and his testimony about warning his host raised factual issues. The court also rejected the argument that the markers were binding because gambling enjoyment could not be restored: the consideration was $700,000 in chips, and if the defense succeeded the casino would get neither the money nor reimbursement.

Certification was proper because the dismissal resolved all of Hakimoglu's affirmative claims and the two sets of claims used different intoxication standards. Undue influence means control sufficient to destroy free agency and compel an act contrary to the person's normal will.

The decisive ground was ratification. Young v. Data Switch, applying Restatement sections 380 and 381 to a severance agreement challenged as coerced eighteen months after signing, distinguished initial voidability from losing the power to avoid once the coercive circumstances ceased. Unreasonable delay, especially while retaining benefits, and conduct inconsistent with disaffirmance can bar avoidance. Intent to ratify can be inferred from affirmative conduct or silence; the question is whether there was an opportunity to disaffirm after the pressure ended, not the person's explanation for failing to do so. The court set no automatic ten-month deadline.

Although Young involved duress and Gengaro alleged undue influence, the court applied the same reasoning because both involve compromised free assent when the agreement is made. Taken together, the revocation period, the requests for payment, the retained benefits and the ten-month delay established ratification.

Shell argued the lease was independent of the dealer agreement and its landlord rights could not be restricted. New Jersey public policy, drawn from Henningsen and Ellsworth Dobbs, opposed grossly unfair provisions imposed through seriously disproportionate bargaining power that tend to injure the public, and motor-fuel distribution had recognized public importance. The Franchise Practices Act prohibited termination, cancellation or nonrenewal without good cause. Its effective date kept it from applying directly to these earlier agreements, but its restrictions reflected an existing public policy addressing longstanding abuses; the court used that policy and did not apply the Act retroactively.

Shell controlled both the supplies and the location, yet Marinello's service and efforts generated the station's clientele and goodwill. Once an operator had invested years building the trade, a threat of nonrenewal left him little practical ability to negotiate. The nominal availability of termination to both sides did not create equal power: Shell could install a replacement and keep the going business, while Marinello would lose his clientele. The almost-at-will provisions were grossly unfair in that setting.

On good cause, the record amply supported the trial court's finding of substantial performance.

The court did not freeze the operational terms; revision to conform to current area dealer practices remained possible. It reserved whether the relationship would survive Marinello's death or disability and what remedy would apply if Shell in good faith chose to operate the station itself.

The court first stated that a municipal police authority may take measures to prevent interference with public order and that respect for human dignity falls within public order. An attraction that infringes dignity can therefore be prohibited even where the municipality has shown no distinctive local circumstances, which rejected the legal premise of the tribunal's decision.

It then applied that principle to the nature of the show. Treating a person with a physical disability as a projectile, while presenting him precisely in that capacity, infringed human dignity by the attraction's very object. The judgment does not rest on incapacity to consent, on a finding of physical injury, or on an inference that all compensated performances undermine dignity.

Examining the applicants' other arguments, the court held that freedom of work and freedom of commerce and industry did not prevent a municipal authority from prohibiting even an otherwise lawful activity where prohibition was the only measure capable of preventing or ending the interference with public order. Because Article L. 131-2 independently justified the ban, the objection that it could not rest on Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights or a November 27, 1991 ministerial circular was ineffective. The tribunal had therefore wrongly annulled the order and awarded compensation.

The brief relies on the official French text; its English explanations are paraphrases, and the conclusions of the commissaire du gouvernement are not reproduced. The casebook uses the case to ask whether dignity can restrict a competent person's freedom to contract, as a public-policy limit that consent does not overcome.

The court agreed with the district about the governing rule: a designated third person's decision on construction disputes can be binding, subject to fraud, a gross mistake necessarily implying bad faith, or a failure of honest judgment. A court may not merely substitute what it regards as a better calculation. But decisions without a reasonable basis, or patently erroneous ones, can constitute the equivalent of bad faith and the necessary gross mistake.

The evidence supported the trial court's finding that Wilscam used Negus-Sweenie's figures without verifying a reasonable relationship to actual costs. RaDec had supplied an accounting that accurately reflected the savings from eliminating imported fill, but Wilscam did not use it. That was more than a disagreement over professional discretion: the method was patently erroneous for the contract change being evaluated.

Because this was a law action tried without a jury, the trial court's findings had the effect of a jury verdict and would be reversed only if clearly wrong. Under that review the gross-mistake conclusion stood, and the district's correct statement of the stricter rule did not require reversal.

The casebook asks whether grossly erroneous but potentially honest judgment can satisfy the bad-faith limitation; the brief notes that the court reasoned by legal equivalence and made no finding of conscious dishonesty.

Submitting the application bound Giunto to the final-decisions clause. Drawing on other contest decisions, the majority recognized that agreed tournament or award decisions remain binding absent fraud, gross mistake or lack of good faith, and a footnote likened the clause to arbitration's function of resolving disputes outside court. The judge had to apply the rules to a puck that entered but did not pass fully through, and because no disqualifying misconduct or error had been pleaded or proved, his decision bound the contestant.

The signed spectator agreement also told Giunto before the shot that the judges would read the original language to require complete passage. He would have remanded for entry of judgment on the jury's verdict.

The casebook presents the case as a problem and says Giunto insisted the puck passed completely through; the brief notes that the opinion instead records his concession that it did not.

The standard attorney-review provision came from a court-approved settlement between the bar and realtors. Only the realtor's notice was subject to the specified delivery methods; any actual notice sufficed for the buyers themselves. The panel inferred that the prescribed methods protected real-estate professionals, while attorney review protected contracting parties from being bound by broker-prepared documents without legal advice. The buyers' own notice right was satisfied, and they sought to enforce a realtor delivery right about which the realtor did not complain.

The court applied the principle that a condition's nonoccurrence may be excused to avoid disproportionate forfeiture unless its occurrence was material to the agreed exchange, weighing the extent of the lost rights, the importance of the risk protected against, and how much protection excusing exact compliance would cost. Strict enforcement would forfeit Guerrero's right to disapprove and enter a different agreement, while the buyers already had the timely actual notice the delivery rule sought to ensure. The procedure was not an individually negotiated term but one imposed by the settlement, which justified more liberal substantial-compliance treatment.

Peterson, Kutzin, Romano and Gaglia were distinguished, because here there was a timely disapproval and actual notice and only the method deviated. The panel refused the amicus request to revise the standard clause for modern communications.

The brief notes that the casebook's account reverses the parties: it was the seller's counsel who disapproved and the buyers who sought specific performance.

Counsel for the seller argued that each covenant was general and independent, one promise being consideration for the other, and relied on older authorities including Pordage v. Cole and Blackwell v. Nash to say that the purchaser's remedy lay in a separate action. He also suggested that the buyer had to act first by choosing what conveyance he wanted.

Kenyon thought the case clear in strict law and in justice. The reciprocal acts were to occur together: the seller would receive the price on conveyance, and the buyer the estate on payment. It would be unreasonable to make one party part with the whole consideration and rely on a separate suit against a possibly insolvent counterparty. He accepted the older principle that dependent covenants require the plaintiff to perform or offer performance, but rejected applying it as if a mere exchange of promises made the duties independent.

Buller likewise reasoned that conveyance and payment were by the nature of the sale acts to be done together, invoking Mansfield's explanation that neither side was to give the other personal credit. He answered the buyer-first argument by pointing out that Goodisson first had to take up the copyhold himself. Grose supported asking whether in reality the seller had to act first or the performances were concurrent, rather than resolving dependency by technical wording.

Counsel for Evans argued that the January notice conclusively refused performance, discharged the sellers' duty to deliver, and entitled them to sue at once, so that they could have sold the wheat by sample in transit and should not benefit from a further fall in the market. Alderson asked how that could be distinguished from Leigh v. Paterson, which emphasized that a mutually made contract remains open unless the plaintiff assents to ending it.

Lord Abinger found no ground to reduce the damages, considered Leigh directly applicable, and adopted its reasoning. Parke gave the fuller explanation. If the sellers could have sued immediately after the notice, the notice-date measure might follow, but no such action lay before the delivery time. Evans's undertaking was to be ready and willing to receive and pay for the goods when the contract required; an earlier declaration that he would refuse did not itself break that undertaking, because he could still accept when the wheat was due. The sellers therefore had to wait and see. Parke qualified the point: the notice was ineffective before the receipt date unless the seller acted on it in the meantime and rescinded the contract, which these sellers had not done. Alderson said again that Leigh governed, and Gurney concurred.

The brief notes that this reasoning preceded the anticipatory-breach doctrine associated with Hochster and should not be restated as a modern, universal bar on suing for anticipatory repudiation. The casebook uses the case to illustrate waiting for performance despite a refusal and compares later authorities, including Roehm v. Horst.

CT-ADDITIONAL-CM-B3-094:
Seacoast undertook to supply gas to a federal housing project from April 15, 1947, to June 15, 1948. The government's claim described an October 7 letter declaring that Seacoast would cancel as of November 15 because of an asserted government breach; the report elsewhere refers to an October 24 letter, an inconsistency the brief preserves. The government immediately disputed any right to stop performance and said it would solicit other bids if the refusal persisted.

By November 6 bids had been received, with Trion the low bidder. Zell, president of both Seacoast and Trion, attended the bid opening and refused a request to withdraw Seacoast's notice. Regional counsel sent Seacoast a registered letter addressed to Zell saying that unless the government received a written withdrawal and assurance of continued performance within three days, it would accept Trion's bid and hold Seacoast and its performance bond responsible. Seacoast did not respond within that period. Zell again refused to retract on November 10, and the government accepted Trion's bid. On November 13 Zell told regional counsel that Seacoast admitted it had no right to cancel and rescinded its notice. The new contract was signed on November 17; the uncontradicted evidence attributed the delay to Trion's failure to furnish its bond sooner.

The court recognized the general principle that renunciation of an executory contract may allow the other party to act on a breach before performance is due. But it rejected the claim that Bernstein's letter necessarily ended the contract as a matter of law. Whether the correspondence and the parties' understanding justified treating it as a renunciation was properly left to the jury; the defendants had themselves asked for submission of that issue, and the instructions given covered it.

More decisively, by rejecting the replacement paper because an existing signed contract already governed, the defendants retained their contractual rights instead of accepting a termination. That election operated on both parties: Bernstein remained liable if he failed to perform, and the defendants remained obliged to furnish the theater. They could not keep a right to insist on his performance while treating their own duty as discharged. The brief notes that the holding depends on that affirmative response and does not declare that every refusal of changed terms prevents reliance on a repudiation.

On damages, the ordinary recovery would be the profits from Bernstein's half of receipts after expenses, but the receipts from the four performances were speculative and not provable. The defendants argued that only nominal damages remained. The court disagreed because that ignored a separately proved loss: the jury could find the expenditures were legitimately incurred for performance, were within the parties' contemplation, and became a loss through the refusal of the theater. The court would not assume Bernstein would have lost those amounts even had the defendants performed.

Schilling and Klingler successfully appealed their suspensions to the circuit court and were reinstated. In a 1972 decision the Wisconsin Supreme Court reversed an award of full back pay without deductions for outside earnings and remanded. On remand the trial court deducted Schilling's outside earnings in full, found that both officers had made reasonable and diligent efforts to find other work, and denied prejudgment interest. In 1974 the Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed the orders.

A discharged or suspended employee must seek other employment, and the employer may receive credit for earnings actually obtained or that could have been obtained. The employee need not seek or accept work of a different or inferior kind. The employer bears the burden of establishing both a lack of reasonable and diligent efforts and the availability of suitable work. The officers were not necessarily limited as a matter of law to police jobs, since each had other work experience, but the employer introduced no evidence that alternative work was available during the disputed periods. The trial court's findings of diligent effort were not against the great weight and clear preponderance of the evidence. A precise statement about a differently configured product does not automatically become a warranty about the buyer's actual boat. The court contrasted an earlier jewelry case in which an appraisal described the very diamonds being sold. The brochure, by contrast, identified no specific speed or other measurable characteristic; section 2-313(2) preserves the distinction between an affirmation or description and an opinion commending the goods, and on this record the sentence was commendation.

On merchantability, the court considered two statutory aspects separately. For acceptance in the trade, Crow offered no evidence of the offshore-boat trade's standard or that a substantial segment of buyers would reject a boat of this capability; his testimony that travel to the Gulf Stream took too long described his own preferences. For fitness for ordinary purposes, the evidence of actual offshore fishing and substantial engine hours undermined any inference of general unfitness, and his explanation that many hours were spent on repairs did not prove otherwise.

On fitness for a particular purpose, Crow identified the purpose as offshore fishing in a boat capable of thirty miles per hour. He had discussed fishing and speed, but the record did not show that Atherton knew a slower boat was unacceptable to him, and that failure defeated the claim. Because every ground of liability failed, the court did not decide the damages questions. The court also discussed implied warranty, in a passage the casebook omits.
CT-CB-0026:
The court accepted the ordinary preference for damages in transactions involving chattels but found special circumstances. Sparrow had turned a green horse into a trained roping prospect through his own time and skill, which gave this animal a distinctive value to him. A payment of market value would not supply the promised performance in an adequate form, so he was entitled to Keno himself. The court did not find that all horses are irreplaceable for every buyer.

The court quoted Arkansas Statutes section 68-1468, which authorized specific performance of a seller's broken undertaking to deliver specific or ascertained goods when a court of equity thought the remedy appropriate, as an additional basis for relief. The statute did not make the remedy automatic; the inquiry into why damages were insufficient remained necessary. This statutory discussion is in the full opinion but not in the casebook excerpt.

Morris's objection that delivery was conditional on a good job turned on disputed testimony. Both parties had testified before the chancellor, and the court sustained his finding for Sparrow. It announced no general test for satisfaction conditions.

On accord and satisfaction, the check paid precisely the cash balance both sides acknowledged, Sparrow never abandoned his claim to Keno, and Morris himself was still discussing delivery of the horse at the bank. There was thus no clear basis for reading the check as an agreed replacement for the whole compensation package. The words paid in full must be read in their setting. The court recognized that a disputed money amount, knowingly accepted in full settlement, might have a different consequence, but did not decide that case.
